The precision required for resolving the issue corresponds to a significant fraction of the neutrino energy. In the study of high-energy physics at colliders, particularly in searches for resonant signatures of new physics, specific final states can be difficult to identify due to their complex nature. The challenge arises from massive particles decaying into multiple jets, a phenomenon referred to as a "jet vertex". To improve the detection of these signals, researchers have developed an advanced method of "top tagging", which involves analyzing the jet vertex to distinguish it from standard jet patterns using distinct variables. To gauge the reliability of these tags, researchers employed two different methods to determine the accuracy of the tags. One method, referred to as the "truth matching discriminator", involves comparing the tags to their underlying particle sources, while another, referred to as the "fake rate cut flow", involves measuring the frequency of certain particle combinations based on their likelihood of occurrence. By applying Shapley values to the truth matching discriminator, researchers were able to quantify the influence of certain particle patterns on top tagging accuracy. The findings of this study indicate that top tagging can effectively distinguish between signal types, with signal efficiencies ranging from 20% to 40%, depending on the signal mass. Furthermore, the tags are shown to retain their reliability when applied to distinct sets of particle patterns, suggesting that certain particle patterns have a relatively small influence compared to others, as revealed by Shapley values. This research defines a basic vocabulary for modeling the structure of Organizational Views (OVs) in a formal context. It then develops a method for enhancing these models by integrating additional information. The ultimate goal is to provide a comprehensive framework for various OV implementations, promoting communication and comparison among researchers and practitioners.

To enhance robustness in the dynamic real-world, policy gradient reinforcement learning methods utilize a technique called experience replay. This research introduces a novel approach that leverages the variability in the replay buffer to accelerate convergence. The algorithm prioritizes the re-playback of high-variability episodes and modifications within the high-variability trajectories, aiming to decrease variance and accelerate convergence. Experimental results validate our approach, demonstrating a significant convergence speed-up on average, specifically of approximately 2x, 3x, and 6x, in the policy gradient reinforcement learning settings of CartPole, MuJoCo, and HalfCite, respectively.

Two new methods, the superbosonization of the Gaussian functional and the generalized Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, are employed to derive the $1/N$ expansion of the free energy density of a specific model involving an O(N) symmetric phi^4 theory in d dimensions. The results from these methods are found to be highly symmetric and singular when simplified, and accurately reproduce the known results of the 1/N expansion. The approaches are found to be equivalent and result in the same quartic action for gauge bosons through an integration over auxiliary fields.

Recent studies in Naive Motion Planner (NMP) for spatiotemporal predictive learning have shown some success; however, this approach only relies on position information derived from encoder outputs, neglecting crucial motion details. As a result, even when the NMP framework is used, safe navigation proves challenging. In this research, we focus on capturing motion details in dynamic environments to facilitate predictable movement. We introduce a module that incorporates motion characteristics captured from diverse datasets, offering a feasible solution for real-time implementation. Experimental evaluations show that our approach produces motion paths comparable to those generated by state-of-the-art motion models. Furthermore, the proposed motion feature also enables significant improvements in obstacle avoidance when combined with the NMP framework.

This work introduces Josephine, an experimental runtime library that blends the benefits of Rust's static analysis and compile-time safety features with the dynamic nature of other languages, leveraging JavaScript. Josephine acts as a bridge between Rust and JavaScript, enabling safe data sharing between the two languages while securely handling interdependent data in a manner similar to Rust's ownership model. At its core, Josephine promotes high-level programming, shielding developers from low-level implementation details and efficiently managing memory, ultimately aiming to promote sound programming practices. This paper outlines Josephine's key safety mechanisms, documents preliminary benchmarks and performance data, and discusses lessons learned from developing the library, including challenges encountered during programming and their root causes.

The investigation into neutrinoless double-beta decay serves as a probe for searching for Majorana neutrinos, and a cutting-edge method for this probe would be using colliders to precisely measure the mass of Majorana neutrino states. If new colliders are built, scientists can use them to find the masses of Majorana neutrino states by studying how these states are produced. Since collider experiments typically measure particles' longitudinal velocities, researchers can identify states based on their velocities. In a large collider, there would be many states produced concurrently, and their subsequent decays would result in a complex mixture of states. Within the framework of the standard model extended by the effective field theory of dark matter, our study shows that this mixture of states will influence measurements, resulting in states that seem to have inconsistent velocities. In a realistic scenario of a 100-TeV collider, our simulation indicates that this effect could reduce the accuracy of mass measurement by a factor of 4 for low-mass states and failing to improve it for high-mass states compared to a hypothetical collider designed to optimize the measurement of these states.

A proposed system combines polar codes and list decoding through belief propagation to create a diversified decoding approach. This method has been assessed using a code with a code size of $N=2^{16}$ and message length of $K=1$, which was generated using a binary memoryless symmetric channel with a transition probability of $p=0.5$. Under these conditions, the simulation yielded an error vector weight decoding failure probability of less than $10^{-8}$ after eight iterations. Notably, this method requires significantly fewer iterations than conventional methods, which is an essential factor on practical hardware due to the computational expense associated with multiple-path decoding in high-temperature settings.

This research explores the diffraction patterns of merged astronomical images, forming an new category of diffraction patterns. Analytic expressions are derived for the central valley depth, location, and radius of combined images and their behavior is examined numerically. An analytical-fractional fourier technique is employed to analyze these diffraction patterns, providing insights into the number of images that can be combined based on system resolution.

Building upon the established knowledge that irreversible plastic deformation contributes significantly to the fracture resilience of crystalline materials, we have further refined the theoretical framework. Through linear elasticity-plasticity coupling and considering both plastic strains and dislocations as primary sources of deformation, we have developed a model that correlates the surface dislocation density with plastic strains. This effort has led to the establishment of a new parameter, $\hat{\sigma}$, which integrates both surface dislocation density and plastic strains to assess fracture resilience. Additionally, we have defined both intrinsic and extrinsic fracture resilience based on $\hat{\sigma}$, which respectively focus on material properties and microstructure arrangements. This new framework is supported by microplasticity theory and dislocation theory, and is intended to provide comprehensive understanding of crystalline materials undergoing irreversible deformation.

It is demonstrated that adding multiple independent SLE curves driven by separate Gaussian fields to a conformal loop ensemble or a Gaussian free field results in the vorticity field of these SLEs converging to a universal limit which is the field derived from the Ginzburg-Landau model's order parameter near its second-order phase transition point.

For the Cauchy problem of the Navier-Stokes equations under periodic boundary conditions, we examine the well-posedness issue for the vorticity $\omega$ up to time $T_0(T_0>0)$ in the context of the maximum $L_2(0,T_0);W)$ norm. The properties of the solution are identified in a transformation of the data, which remains smooth in the sense of Schauder. The existence of a gain-of-regularity estimate is established for the solution of the linearized equation in the maximum $L_2(0,T_0);H^1)$ norm. The behavior of the solution is studied as $T_0\to\infty$, and its application is related to the question of the global smooth solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations under the condition \eqref{NS-2}.

To ensure that quantum computers operate correctly, we need to validate their output by checking if it matches the expected results. However, verifying these outputs is highly complex due to the rapid growth in the data amount with each additional qubit involved. Current best approaches run in the O(2^n) time complexity, where n represents the number of qubits used. In this research, we present a new verification method with a linear time complexity in relation to the number of qubits used, thereby addressing the growth issue for multi-qubit computations. Our approach leverages the ability to create intermediate classical results during the verification process through simulating intermediate classical states. Furthermore, we take advantage of the ability to conduct selective verification on specific output bits while ignoring the rest. Additionally, we take into account that in most cases, the input bits are random, thereby establishing a baseline for randomness in the input bits. Lastly, we also present a new approach for simulating the intermediate classical states with a time complexity in relation to the number of qubits used, thereby addressing the challenge for multi-qubit computations.

This study presents a novel framework for establishing trust in IoT systems employing blockchains. It showcases the practical application of a system in a food supply chain and highlights the advantages of using intelligent contracts. The proposed framework utilizes specialized devices called oracles to address the limitations associated with blockchain data integrity, specifically non-reversible transactions. Intelligence within the system is provided by pre-programmed intelligent contracts. The framework was tested in a food supply chain setting and proved to enhance transparency, allowing for the flexible integration of new features through distributed ledger technology (DLT).

Our approach to generating synthetic, lifelike cell shapes is inspired by the success of neural networks in creating realistic images of plants and animals. The conventional method for modeling cell forms is limited, as it relies on a predetermined shape space that can only generate cell shapes so sophisticated. In order to break free from these constraints, we have developed an alternative representation of cell shapes using implicit neural networks, allowing for the limitless creation of complex forms. The model learns to decompose a three-dimensional space into areas with corresponding organ shapes by assigning a scalar value to each point, and can reproduce cells with defects with high accuracy given just a few examples. Given its ability to freely generate complex forms, we believe this representation has the potential to significantly expand the scope of synthetic cell modeling, ultimately leading to the synthesis of cells with extended lifespans.

The proliferation of digital documentation has led to an alarming rise in the number of people with visual and visual-related impairments. As a result, there is an urgent need to adapt existing documentation formats to ensure accessibility for all users, including those with impairments. In response, IndART project is addressing this gap by providing accessible digital tools for visualizing and sharing Indian artistic content through integrated platforms, digital expositories, and digitalization initiatives. Our research outlines the fundamental requirements for making documentation formats accessible, drawing on our experience with the IndART project.

Recently introduced autoregressive language models like BERT and RoBERTa have set new performance benchmarks in several key linguistic tasks. However, these models suffer from a fundamental limitation, as they only consider previous context when predicting subsequent text, thereby rendering future context unusable in such predictions. In response, we are introducing XLNet, a generalized pretraining approach that reconciles the limitations of autoregressive and generative models. As a result, XLNet is capable of leveraging both autoregressive and generative models to learn more robust language representations that achieve significantly improved results. When fine-tuned on the GLUE suite of linguistic tasks, our model surpasses recent state-of-the-art outcomes by 2.2 percentage points. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that XLNet's innovative optimization objective can be an effective method for enhancing deep sequential models.

We have developed detailed models to account for stellar activity in low-resolution transit spectroscopy, which also takes into account the influence of stellar rotation. Utilizing genetic algorithms, our analysis reveals that unmodeled stellar activity effects can significantly obscure planetary atmospheric features, making accurate exoplanetary characterization in low-resolution spectra highly susceptible to errors. Notably, our study indicates that high-resolution spectroscopy appears to be an effective method to mitigate the effects of stellar activity, providing a means to uncover the composition of exoplanetary atmospheres. We have demonstrated this approach with HST/COS spectra of the exoplanet HAT-P-18b, which also showcased the limitations of low-resolution spectra in identifying atmospheric features comparable to those found on Earth. Additionally, our analysis also includes a comparison with UV spectra of GJ 1214 b, which remains an active area of research.

We establish a theorem that ensures, given any Riemann surface and a smoothly
adapted metric with vanishing Gauss-Bonnet curvature, an Anomaly-Free, Constant
Curvature metric can be developed through a series of iterations. This Anomaly-Free,
Constant Curvature metric is provided with a holomorphic metric norm and a Green's
function, or, in the case of a metric with positive constant curvature, an analytic
metric norm can be established.

A crucial aspect of a centipede's movement is its ability to navigate through water with high efficiency, particularly when it's dark and its vision is limited, prompting research into its dynamics.  To explore the dynamics of this motion, researchers employed detailed 3D digital models of a selected species, the forest centipede (Scolopendra marmoreus).  By replicating the model centipedes' movements on a water-like virtual surface, it was discovered that their unique gait allowed them to cover a significant distance while leaving minimal marks on the surface, with some models leaving no marks at all.  This ability is attributed to the centipede's leg action that creates vortex rings on the surface, allowing it to move with high speeds of up to 0.36 body lengths per second.  This gait, where the centipede's leg action forms a water column that supports the centipede's movement, is found to be distinct from previous theories that it was based on gait patterns such as the "metachronic pattern" or "alternating gait".  This new finding shows significantly higher speeds when compared with previous theories and other swimming styles, such as the frog's style of movement, that it was thought were the fastest previous styles of movement, when in fact they were just the second fastest.  This new style has been named "locomotion dynamics" and other theories have been named "gait patterns".  This new style

A novel software called DisasterSim, built on the FEniCS project, is introduced for simulations involving delicate and destructive dispersive wave interactions. DisasterSim is used to model devastating ocean wave behaviors such as those triggered by a massive asteroid impact. Key aspects of dispersive wave interactions are efficiently resolved, including the intricate coupling of shallow water waves and seismic activity. This integration is achieved by combining Stokes theory with linear elasticity and buoyancy, resulting in a computational framework that can predict a range of extreme ocean behaviors, from the initial seismic activity to a catastrophic tsunami resulting from a massive asteroid impact. DisasterSim is comprised of multiple flexible and extensible modules that are open-sourced and available for modification. This flexibility enables a high level of precision in simulating various scenarios, allowing for a range of asteroid sizes and materials to be simulated with or without pre-existing seismic activity. DisasterSim is used to model a variety of scenarios, offering a range of possible disaster scenarios and providing insight into the connection between asteroid characteristics and resulting wave patterns.

Using early JWST data from the NorthEast Volume Deep Extragalactic Survey, researchers have identified and characterized a unique class of extremely dusty galaxies (DGs) with low optical brightness. These galaxies are less prominent than typical luminous star-forming galaxies, yet their infrared flux suggests massive star-forming activity or substantial dust obscuration. Statistical analysis indicates that such galaxies were prevalent at $z=2-5$ with a $\sim$4% volume density at $z \sim 3.5$, accounting for 30% of star-forming galaxies with star formation rates above 10 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-2}$. By analyzing spectral energy distributions, the team found that these galaxies have high dust masses and extremely dusty environments similar to extremely metal-rich galaxies. Notably, 85% of such galaxies were discovered in the optical, featuring little to no Lyman break features, indicating a high level of dust-limited absorption at rest-frame UV wavelengths, or alternatively, high residual continuum levels at the Lyman limit. These galaxies are expected to significantly contribute to measurements of their respective redshift distributions due to their dominant dust-corrected luminosities, or constraints on neutral hydrogen absorption within their vicinity.

This research focuses on understanding the fundamental laws governing seven-dimensional space-time, characterized by two distinct features: the presence of Einstein's general theory of gravitation and an additional topological component, which emerges from a fundamental two-form field describing the unique properties of space-time. By solving the fundamental equations derived from this system, we uncover solutions that can describe static gravitational fields with varying forms depending on the field's decomposition with respect to a preferred frame of reference. Additionally, we analyze the properties of space-time at its event horizon, which gives rise to a novel black hole solution, and we also discuss its asymptotic behavior for the scenarios of flat and hyperbolic geometries. Furthermore, we determine a relationship between the mass and angular momentum parameters by applying the asymptotic field equations, which in turn allows us to classify these black hole solutions based on different topological conditions.

This research investigates the dynamic behavior of two-dimensional disks and varying masses confined within a parallel channel. The studies are conducted in a framework where boundary conditions are allowed to change over time. A new set of numerical techniques is created to analyze problems involving evolving boundaries, and these techniques are then used to explore a previously unstudied scenario in which disks and masses are inserted into a channel at specific intervals. The results demonstrate a recurring pattern in the behavior of these objects as more and more items accumulate in the channel, and show that this pattern gives rise to a unique form of dynamic that occurs when the channel becomes clogged. Additionally, varying the mass of the objects affects how they accumulate in the channel, leading to complex and often irregular arrangements, both periodically and unpredictably.

To better comprehend the diverse forms of El Ni\~no-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), researchers combine statistical and data-driven approaches with distinctive classification methods. By integrating multi-scale pattern recognition techniques, scientists analyze the various kinds of ENSO into categories such as Standard, Co-Occurrence, and Elevated types. This research utilizes daily precipitation data to characterize the unique patterns of low and elevated precipitation around the world associated with each EENSO type. Using daily scales, the study leverages spatial and temporal data analysis to further differentiate standard and co-occurrence ENSO types. It identifies distinct regional and temporal connections between these kinds of EENSO and precipitation patterns at different latitudes, primarily in South America and west Africa.

To utilize the potential of real-time, non-invasive optical measurement in analyzing complex polymer and cellulose gel formations, it is crucial to understand its limitations. Previously, researchers were unable to apply this method due to uncertainty surrounding non-affine strand movements impacting optical properties. A new approach has now overcome these limitations by employing picosecond pulse illumination to reveal gel formations at the molecular level. The discovered power law in PS polymer solution and cellulose gel suggests that self-similarity in optical properties and gel structure occurs across various time frames, explaining their observed gelation patterns. The discovered power law in cellulose also correlates with established models of network formation. This new method has further revealed that PS gelation primarily involves the mobility of monomers, whereas cell wall cellulose undergoes degradation through the breakdown of individual crystalline structures. The discovered power law also facilitated the measurement of gel properties during deep seawater extrusion, a process critical in preserving cellulose content for industrial applications.

In this research, we establish two mathematical frameworks for a single population with age considerations, taking into account behavioral responses due to environmental pollution, under the assumptions of Monod response and the logistic growth model. Our models rely on ordinary differential equations and have been proven to be well-posed. Using these frameworks, we explore the long-term effects of pollution on the population, as well as how environmental quality impacts population dynamics. Our analysis also examines the stability of the population in different environmental contexts, ultimately leading to a model that integrates the effects of environmental pollution, age structure, and behavioral responses.

A new approach to dealing with implications in logic has been developed, involving hypersequents that allow for certain 'unsafe' steps to be cancelled out. This has led to considerations of 'contracting' hypersequents, where certain logical operations become less versatile. We investigate the decision-making process for certain families of logics, including some that allow for explosion and have both 'contractible' and 'non-contractible' versions. The decision-making process raises complexities, with some versions undecidable, while 'alleviated' versions (allowing for explosion but not cancelling it) become decidable. However, this has come at a cost: instead of having polynomial-time solutions, the decision-making process takes at least quadratic time when considering the size of inputs.

Deep learning training methods have been very successful in improving the accuracy of graph classification. One key feature of graph classification is its ability to expand knowledge by incorporating more labeled graphs, although this is a challenging task due to the problem's scale and diversity. Existing graph classification methods typically scale poorly when dealing with a large number of graphs, and new techniques, such as graph generation and graph clustering, often compromise accuracy. To address this issue, this paper proposes a new approach called HyperExpan, which uses a compact hyperbolic embedding that allows it to expand classification knowledge efficiently by scaling up to various graph numbers. HyperExpan achieves this by using a distance-based model to group graphs, thereby reducing the complexity of the graph classification problem. Moreover, HyperExpan uses a hyperbolic embedding that enables it to accurately predict node and graph labels, and its performance is further improved by incorporating edge information. HyperExpan's accuracy and efficiency are validated through extensive testing using eight, sixteen, and forty graph datasets.

The accuracy of quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods for calculating intermolecular interaction energies can be enhanced by accounting for external electromagnetic fields. This principle was demonstrated in prior research using the Austin-Morris-Cohen (AMC) model to describe electric field effects in high-accuracy QMC calculations. This work builds on that foundation by testing the AMC model in conjunction with a wide range of wavefunction types for molecular dimers, specifically the 66 (S66) set, which are further divided into two groups based on complexity. This research compares predicted interaction energies, considering variations in molecular orientation, pair separation, and electric field strength, against experimental data and coupled-cluster calculations, showing strong agreement for dimers consisting of non-polar and polar monomers, including associations and dispersive interactions, but notable discrepancies for dimers consisting of polar monomers, including hydrogen-bonded complexes, at higher electric field strengths.

The concept of ambiguity has seen significant expansion in recent machine learning advancements, referring to the uncertainty inherent in data classification and decision-making processes. Despite its growing presence, the ambiguity concept remains underutilized in predictive maintenance scheduling for Industry 4.0 settings. This research aims to improve model robustness by incorporating ambiguity into scheduling, and a novel approach for incorporating ambiguity into the multivariate Gaussian probability function is presented. However, conventional metrics, including mean squared error and R-squared, are ineffective in quantifying ambiguity. This paper proposes the adoption of the Wasserstein distance as a superior metric for evaluating ambiguity. Furthermore, the paper explores the impact of ambiguity on convolutional neural network training, demonstrating that increased ambiguity yields better prediction results. Ambiguity can also be optimized by balancing the use of informative and noisy data, and it is found that using 10% noisy data in an imbalance dataset yields the best prediction results, exceeding that of informative data-only models.

This paper introduces a key component in cyber-physical systems, specifically for control systems, and discusses its impact on system robustness from an STL perspective. Traditional stability analysis focuses on ensuring a system remains safe under all possible conditions, but this concept is challenging to implement when using a time-boundary logic like STL. We resolve this issue by breaking down an STL formula into its core components - a primary statement and the temporal component - and examining how they interact in the context of robustness. This approach enables us to develop a framework for evaluating robustness by focusing on the toughest challenges (sensitivity points) that a system faces and the time periods where it must perform optimally to remain secure (critical times). We illustrate this method with a couple of classic control systems and show its effectiveness through verification and optimization procedures.

A newly developed method for utilizing network-centralized time-series data is presented, centered around an accelerometer-based system featuring 50 devices scattered across an approximate 200m x 100m area. The approach leverages the synergy of local feature extraction and global pattern analysis to identify an object's presence within the surroundings. The system primarily relies on machine learning, employing principal component analysis for dimensionality reduction, to detect an object of unknown composition. When a given time frame is queried, the system calculates distances between learned models and a real-time feature map, enabling timely and accurate object detection. The combination of local and global features yields robustness against sensor data loss and temporal inconsistency, as well as detection superiority when compared to conventional solutions.

We consider a specified nonlinear diffusion type equation defined on a complete manifold and obtain local and global gradient estimates for the solution, assuming certain growth and boundary conditions are met.

To explore the properties of faint radio sources, we analyzed the Faint Radio Sources Catalog from NOEMA's observations of the BOOTES-1N galaxy cluster, specifically looking at sources with flux densities between 0.5 and 5 mJy/beam. We focused on compact objects with sizes smaller than 1 kpc, and by examining multiple sources of the same objects, we were able to quantify several properties such as radio luminosity, excitation, and H$\alpha$ emission. We discovered a correlation between these sources' properties and their size, specifically radio luminosity and excitation, with larger sources exhibiting higher values. Additionally, we found that one in five sources exhibited highly excited emission, indicating that these sources' ionized gas is highly excited. Furthermore, we estimated that about 30% of sources exhibit far-infrared (FIR) emission excess, specifically from star formation processes, with larger sources accounting for a significant portion of this phenomenon. Finally, we were able to quantify the FIR to radio flux density ratio, specifically at 20 kpc sources, and our results suggest that this ratio is similar to what has been reported previously, about 5.0.

This work extends the application of Hidden Markov Models to analyze the trustworthiness of safety-critical systems, focusing specifically on their resistance to hacking.  A new mathematical model, known as the Abstract Concealed Markov Model, is introduced to characterize systems with hidden functional behaviors and concealed attacks.  Data flow diagrams are employed to formally define the data transmission rules and establish a comprehensive framework for HMM and ACMM algebraic expressions.  A category theoretic construction is presented to incorporate heterogeneous uncertainties, including probabilistic, deterministic, and imprecise models, into the ACMM system architecture.  Building upon this framework, a multi-layered trust network is proposed to model complex systems, encompassing inherent trust in their hardware, acquired trust through testing, and assumed trust based on design specifications.  A practical application is demonstrated through a case study analyzing the potential vulnerabilities of the ARM v7l processor's cryptographic module.

This study explores pattern coherence in spatial patterns exhibiting dynamic
coherence, a property found extensively in various systems. To quantify pattern
coherence, a novel measure called pattern coherence is introduced, combining
both global and local entropy principles. This novel approach is applied to
kink/antikink wave collisions, showcasing its ability to capture essential
aspects of coherent pattern behavior. By analyzing pattern coherence along with
other previously reported measures such as the coherence order parameter and
global coherence, pattern coherence's relationships with these other quantities
are systematically investigated and documented. Furthermore, the pattern
coherence schedule is compared with key stages in the process of pattern
formation.

We introduce a novel framework, Flexible Scattering Phenomenology (FSP), an extension of the original YAML-based phenomenology used in the Yale Linear Collider Compact Enclosure (YLCCE) software. FSP enhances this model with Python's extensive capabilities, offering increased flexibility through the use of optional parameters with default values defined by the @dataclass and typing.NamedTuple classes. It also enables users to define and utilize custom types of scattering amplitudes. FSP incorporates the ability to generate, save, manipulate, and match WaffleCards (scattering amplitude tables) as well as read v2 YukawaLP parameters. We illustrate FSP's capabilities by creating a set of novel scattering amplitudes with hidden properties and generating corresponding WaffleCards. We also showcase YLCCE's execution with FSP in a multi-user collaborative environment.

This paper presents a theoretical study where we examine the thermodynamic effects on a blackbody that's influenced by the Casimir effect. We investigate how radiation and matter interact under conditions where the Casimir effect has an impact, and also explore the thermodynamic properties of a system consisting of two unipolar centers that are affected by this phenomenon. We derive equations for internal energy, entropy, and entropy generation rate under these conditions, and then conduct comprehensive analyses of various parameters. We demonstrate that the Casimir effect has a profound impact on entropy generation, and also demonstrate the inherent characteristics of this process. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between entropy generation rate and scattering frequency under conditions where the Casimir effect is present.

Research has been conducted to assess the impact of k-anonymity on location privacy. A key element often overlooked in k-anonymity is the estimation of the location of an individual, which is crucial in k-anonymity. This study introduces the combination of anonymization and location estimation as a novel approach to location privacy. A synthetic location track is created by generating random Gaussian probabilities for locations, while an actual track is anonymized to regions rather than specific points. As a key innovation, our method considers the probabilities of locations, which are used to estimate the location of an individual. A comparison was made between this new approach and a system using time-only information to anonymize location tracks, demonstrating that our method can reduce the aggregation of locations while maintaining a higher accuracy in estimated location comparison to the original track.

A highly advanced representation of 3D point clouds enables accurate place recognition even with intense noise and disordered data organization. In this research, we present NDT-Transformer, a model that pairs the Normal Distribution Transform depiction with the transformer architecture for localized places in a large-scale environment. Our approach combines global feature extraction using the normal distribution transform (NDT) with a global attention mechanism, allowing it to capture global context and relationships between grid cells. Deep transformer architecture helps the model learn complex representations of transformed space representations. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the indoor outdoor loop closure dataset and KITTI dataset.

A key objective in neuroimaging is to establish connections between brain regions.  These connections can be derived from resting-state functional MRI data and are often represented as correlated activity between different brain regions.  However, given the amount of noise present, it's unclear whether observed correlations are genuine or simply a result of chance.  To address this issue, various statistical tests used to determine the significance of these correlations have been developed, including multiple family-wise correction and false discovery rate control.  However, when it comes to predicting behavioral or clinical outcomes based on brain function, accuracy is measured by techniques such as cross-validation.  Predictive models that rely on neural networks are particularly effective in cross-validation but have no connection to the traditional family-wise error family used for inference by authors such as Nichols and Hutton.  This has led to a disconnect between traditional significance testing and prediction tasks, with concerns arising around how to reconcile these disparate results and whether there is a link between significant findings and predictive accuracy.  To address this gap, a unified framework for measuring knowledge accuracy is developed by drawing on both frequentist and Bayesian approaches.  This new framework is applied to data from the MultiSite Neuroimaging Clinical Collective, where it examines the relationship between brain function and behavior across 222 participants and assesses the role of spatial constraints in modeling connectivity.  This unified framework seeks to integrate inference and prediction, with implications for understanding the statistical strength of brain function and its role in prediction.

In a single-hop beeping network, identical beeps serve as a shared form of communication. We explore the most efficient ways for mobile agents to convey distinct names through beeps, with a focus on minimizing the overall time required for name exchange. Building on recent research that introduced optimal point-to-point naming protocols, we investigate the effect of introducing a power-saving constraint. Under this constraint, agents can only detect beeps within a specified radius. We show that, despite this limitation and reduction in name distinctness, there remains a non-trivial set of naming schemes. Furthermore, we present an online algorithm that identifies a subset of these schemes which can be implemented with the fewest beeps. We also introduce a new naming scheme for the general beeping model that can be implemented with the fewest beeps overall.

Recent advancements in NLP from textual data have shown significant success on single-lingual data sets but have yet to accurately handle code-mixed data found in languages such as song lyrics and dialogue that combine multiple languages. The main challenge in code-mixed data lies in its tokenized sequence's unpredictable positional meaning where words from different languages have varying levels of importance. To overcome this issue, a new approach using positional encoding based on transition points has been developed to dynamically assign importance to tokens. The proposed model, Transition point based Dynamic and Relative Positional EnCoding, leverages transition points to assign positional encoding and relative encoding for code-mixed data, enhancing the performance of neural networks. The research includes an experimental evaluation that demonstrates the model's superiority on code-mixed data and a detailed analysis of its components. An evaluation was conducted on two datasets, Splits-2 and Splits-3 of LSTMs-2D, and NER-OM data, showing improved performance with transition point based positional encoding compared to static and relative encoding. Additionally, models using background language positional encoding showed lower performance than models using an automatic and simple calculation of positional encoding from data.

The superconducting properties and critical temperature of H3S, a hydride material, are analyzed under high-pressure conditions, varying from 160 to 180 GPa, by examining two distinct models that incorporate a single band or account for a van Hove singularity at the Fermi level. Comparing the two models shows that the single-band model yields lower critical temperatures than the more comprehensive model. As pressure increases, the critical temperature in the single-band model reaches its peak at 174 GPa, whereas the model incorporating the van Hove singularity reaches its peak at 167 GPa. Additionally, our research indicates that isotopic variations have a more pronounced effect on the superconducting properties in the single-band model, with a correlation between and. Conversely, the model incorporating the van Hove singularity exhibits an alternating dependence on isotopic variations.

We investigate a particular motion planning problem involving two objects: a mover and a static obstacle. The mover's objective is to reach a destination on the shortest path possible. However, the mover can create temporary barriers using a limited number of actions to restrict the static obstacle's movement, thereby making the shortest path accessible. We focus on developing an algorithm that computes these artificial barriers and demonstrates its efficiency with theoretical analysis along with empirical validation through diverse test cases.

A visually reliable system is developed that enables robots to reorient themselves based on pre-created 3D maps of simplified surface data, utilizing artificial intelligence-powered feature extraction through deep learning. By incorporating geometric information associated with surfnet features, a more accurate localization framework is established, employing a particle filter method for navigation. Moreover, a key contribution involves the proposal of a semi-supervised feature learning approach, incorporating both labeled data from pre-created maps and unlabeled sensor readings during real-time operation. This framework initially uses an unsupervised model to automatically detect distinctive features, thereby streamlining computational requirements by diminishing the number of potential data points for consideration. Nevertheless, further support is derived from user-provided labels to fine-tune the model through additional training. Consequently, the developed system successfully integrates user input in an efficient manner, thereby enhancing overall performance by combining geometric information with traditional image-based techniques, thereby enhancing overall reliability. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of this approach, demonstrating robust navigation even in complex scenarios with significant changes in lighting conditions over time.

In MIMO networks where users can switch, we developed an approach that combines user selection and precoding. By modeling user choice as a binary variable and incorporating it into the precoding design, we reformulated the problem as a joint optimization task. To solve this issue, we introduced a new method using Group LASSO via alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) and applied it to two existing algorithms currently used in literature. Furthermore, we suggested an alternative algorithm tailored to our specific problem. Simulation results showed that our approach surpasses existing methods in terms of channel utilization and user signal quality.

Over a complete arc, a specialized semifield replaces the traditional rational function field. The preimage of this semifield under a continuous map involves replacing non-positive minors with zero and transfinite values. The preimage of an arc after a continuous mapping is being examined. The semifield of rational functions in an arc, with negative minors replaced by zero, has been found to be generated by a limited set of functions over a specific semifield. This note clarifies and simplifies a prior research notion by Cullen, Murphy, and Van Handel, focusing on the convergence of a time-changing process called the Q-process. We demonstrate that for the Q-process, being consistent in path convergence is equivalent to being consistent in the quadratic mean. The original paper's application of this equivalence to prove a diffusive limit in quadratic form is reestablished within this simplified framework.

A combinatorial formula driving a Vassiliev 2-fold invariant of long knots in a tangle ring is provided, with roots stemming from a modified version of Fox's space, coupled with Hatcher's loop and the quasis regularization technique in singular cohomology theory.

The correlation between the magnetic properties and the structural arrangement within $p$-wave superconductors is still not fully understood. The presence of spin-triplet superconductivity in C$_{11}$ and C$_{12}$ coefficients indicates that lithium iron arsenide, a material with unique properties where magnetism and superconductivity coexist, may be unstable against anisotropic strain under certain conditions. However, our findings show that the material does not become unstable under strain in any orientation when considered in its experimentally observed state. The material also remains stable when considered in its high-pressure tetragonal phase, but only if spin-triplet correlations are relatively weak. If such correlations are strong, the material then exhibits nematic instability in this phase. The results indicate that the material's resilience to the nematic instability when in its experimentally observed state may be attributed to the material's inherent properties rather than a characteristic of the material's superconducting state. The study also reveals the material's low resilience to the normal state when under strain and in the high-pressure tetragonal phase, which could provide valuable insights into the material's properties.

This analysis combines global particle physics experiments involving 2HDMs and future experiments at LHC, HL-LHC, FCC-ee, FCC-hh, and ILC to determine the best-fit models. With the help of WMAP and Planck constraints, two Higgs doublet models are eliminated, and other candidates are narrowed down. Among the remaining options, four models stand out: type-I and II Higgsless 2HDM, type-Fermion flavor changing 2HDM, and type-II extended scalar third generation model. These models exhibit distinct differences in their responses to various experiments. For example, type-I and II Higgsless 2HDM models are expected to perform well at LHC and HL-LHC, while type-II extended scalar third generation model is more suitable for ILC and FCC-ee.

The study of self-assembling structures is crucial for understanding how molecular assemblies take shape, yet modeling this process is highly complex due to the vast search space involved. This challenge can be overcome by employing neuroevolutionary techniques to optimize model efficiency. When using traditional search methods, optimizing molecular assemblies becomes virtually impossible due to the enormous space involved. In contrast, neuroevolutionary algorithms can effectively train agents to navigate and promote the growth of molecular structures through simulated simulated chemical reactions. This study introduces a novel framework for assemblage modeling that centers on particle behavior. Moreover, it highlights another model, the framework structure, which enables the implementation of a larger-scale search space and more detailed system representation on top of the particle-based structure. This framework has the potential to be adapted to various systems and can even be applied to the simulation of chemical reactions using a graph-based approach. Furthermore, our research reveals that particle structures can be translated into framework structures, allowing for the exploration of particle-based systems. This study also results in the creation of two novel self-assembling systems for benchmark testing using the open-access Game AI researcher's platform for evaluating agent performance. Additionally, our research reveals that particle-based systems exhibit a higher capacity for resilience against imperfect conditions and system resilience can effectively be utilized as an optimization criterion for both particle-based and framework models.

In this work, we examine the relationship between anomalies in gauge theories with a chiral structure and their robust characteristics, specifically focusing on the implications for baryon number conservation in the Standard Model. Our analysis makes use of both classical and quantum combinatorics, which helps us uncover interesting patterns and properties. Furthermore, by representing anomalies as boundaries in the gauge group's quotient space and connecting to topological principles in string theory, we gain further insight into the robust nature of anomalies.

This study contributes towards addressing a long-standing question raised by Tsurumi in 2019: under what conditions does the steady Navier-Stokes equation remain stable in high dimensions? Specifically, we investigate the relationship between input data and resulting output data in terms of certain space and Lp norms. Our key finding is that if a certain combination of these norms exceeds 5/3, then small changes in input data lead to correspondingly large changes in output data. To reach this conclusion, we built on existing work by Alazzawi et al and developed a new representation theorem for continuously operating systems. Our work has implications for understanding how certain non-linear systems behave. Conversely, we discovered that smaller changes are required for these systems, specifically 3/5, to hold true.

At high temperatures, the frequency of a type of sound wave (magnon) in an antiferromagnetic material changes in a way that depends on the direction of propagation and amplitude. Researchers found that when this type of sound wave interacts with other similar waves, it results in a complex phenomenon where the frequency shifts and the material's effective mass changes simultaneously. By analyzing how the material's structure changes in response to this interaction, it has been predicted that the material's critical point will be followed by a phase transition where the material's sublattices begin to move in sync. This phenomenon may be observed in certain compounds made of manganese and have significant implications for the study of these types of materials.

This research introduces two modifications to Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem to enhance its security and workability. Initially, a novel error and decryption algorithm is proposed, combining both error correction and decryption processes, thereby reducing computational complexity. Secondly, a modification is made to Loidreau's secret list by substituting it with a randomly selected subset of codewords from the code, thereby enhancing the system's randomness and security. Additionally, two random lists are implemented, namely the public list and a secret list, both comprising distinct words from the code, with the public list being disclosed publicly, and the secret list being solely accessible to the sender and receiver. Evaluation and analysis of the proposed algorithm were conducted using parameters derived from a extended binary BCH code, and the results compared with Loidreau's original system. Notably, a higher minimum distance between code words was achieved with fewer than 23 errors being detectable and corrected, and the proposed algorithm requiring significantly fewer bytes than Loidreau's original system.

To enhance word representation in large language models like BERT, which is primarily trained using sentence-level contextual information, we introduce a new method for incorporating dictionary-based word meanings. This approach involves assigning a common meaning to a set of words and improves BERT's word representations by promoting their aggregation within the dictionary. Extensive experiments confirm that our method benefits BERT model performance across various tasks. Under the condition that the WordNet dictionary is available, our method allows for zero-shot cross-lingual transfer without requiring any target-language training data. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the proposed method facilitates more accurate lexical semantic representations by aligning BERT word embeddings with their corresponding dictionary meanings.

We examine the characteristics of the largest eigenvalue and certain statistical measures related to the eigenvalues of specific types of matrices, including those that model random geometric structures. These matrices are of a singular nature and have previously been discussed in research related to Laplacian matrices, which describes their eigenvalue behavior but lacks applicability to our current study. In this work, we establish that the behavior of the largest eigenvalue in our context follows that of a standard matrix, and subsequently derive statistical measures related to the eigenvalue distribution. Our results are then validated through numerical experiments. Additionally, we relate our findings to the topology of certain geometric structures, including those that model subspaces in high-dimensional data and have previously been analyzed using a single statistical measure. Our results are validated through numerical experiments and shed light on the existence of a threshold beyond which adding more data does not significantly impact our understanding of the underlying structure.

This paper explores a vulnerability in vertical federated learning caused by strategically designed federal privacy policies that create unexpected data inconsistencies. When detailed data and associated metadata are handled separately during training, a malicious attack can be devised that compromises the learning process, even with an unlimited number of participants and an arbitrarily chosen privacy policy. To illustrate the efficacy of this approach, several Federal Learning configurations are examined, showcasing that our proposed technique can be tailored for each specific use case in order to identify vulnerable scenarios and maximize potential loss. Furthermore, this technique can be fine-tuned and adapted to overcome defenses implemented by researchers, demonstrating both theoretical and practical applicability.

Recent experimental findings regarding B-mesons decaying into particles like protons, antiprotons, and dark matter antibaryons are of considerable interest due to their implications on quantum chromodynamics and dark matter theories. Utilizing a novel approach called QCD light-cone synthesis, predictions for specific branching fractions of certain B-meson decays into protons and dark matter antibaryons have been calculated, with particular focus on a certain type of decay involving a dark matter particle as a quark-gluon color singlet. Three distinct models for the structure of dark matter particles, varying in their composition (quark-like, gluon-like, or a mixture of quarks and gluons known as "gluonon"), have been considered in order to better understand and predict these decays. Key findings from this research include predicted branching fractions of specific B-meson decays – namely $B^0 \rightarrow p \bar X^0$, with $\bar X^0$ representing a type of dark matter particle as a quark-gluon color singlet, and $B^+ \rightarrow p K^0$ or $B^+ \rightarrow p \pi^0$ in conjunction with a certain type of dark matter particle as a quark-gluon color octet. It is estimated that certain types of decay involving dark matter particles as quark-gluon color singlets or nonsinglets would result in a certain type of quantum chromodynamics process occurring

This study introduces an innovative, interrelated model for defending cities against emerging threats that incorporate socio-cyber-physical components. These threats, facilitated by extensive access to sensitive information, are increasingly devastating and difficult to predict. The proposed model develops a strategic resource allocation game that simulates the manager's dilemma in responding to assaults. By extending traditional defense strategies, the framework leverages the concept of network centrality to optimize resource distribution for rescue and recovery efforts following an assault, while also addressing the inherent challenges in resource allocation. The paper showcases the model's efficacy through a real-world city defense simulation in Chicago.

To investigate how black hole phase transitions are affected by a confining environment, we conducted both physical and statistical thermodynamic analyses. Our study focused on the thermodynamic properties of a Schwarzschild black hole enclosed within a cavity using a model where the cavity's boundary is treated as a particle's scattering against a potential wall. This approach helped us clarify the scattering model's previous findings and expand on their relevance to phase transitions. Our analysis revealed that confinement, which limits a black hole's size, doesn't fundamentally alter its phase transition characteristics, although it does affect the transition's duration and thermodynamic behavior. Moreover, our study's results in high-temperature conditions showed concordance with those from physical thermodynamic analyses.

Search engines continuously collect user feedback in the form of marks or ratings for ranked documents. This information is utilized to refine ranking models. In contrast, research on document labeling is relatively limited. We aim to develop a cost-effective method for generating labeled documents. Since creating gold standard labels is impractical, we adopt a self-supervised approach. First, we identify relevant subsets of data by applying bag sampling and analyzing the distribution of labels. Next, we categorize observations into distinct groups and use a tailored loss function to create training sets for model adaptation, ultimately resulting in improved performance. Experimentation with multiple datasets and various noise types demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach.

To effectively train Graph Neural Networks with limited node labels, we introduce EPL, an innovative pseudo-labeling technique that combines supervised and self-supervised learning. EPL starts by utilizing the labeled information to generate pseudo-labels through supervised learning; however, to prevent the model from memorizing these pseudo-labels, it employs a self-supervised loss function to disrupt the model's expectations. This counteraction mechanism allows the model to consistently learn from pseudo-labels without becoming reliant on them. Our experimental outcomes indicate that EPL successfully addresses the issue of limited labels on various graph datasets, surpassing numerous baseline methods, including self-supervised learning strategies.

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma is proposed as a reliable method for independently determining the electron beam's trajectory, complementing diagnostics in plasma beam-line experiments.  This method has been successfully utilized in analyzing data from the AWAKE experiment, where it allowed for the estimation of trajectory information by means of spectroscopic analysis of betatron radiation emitted by electrons deflected through plasma waves.  By combining both direct photodiode measurements and those after a 2.5-meter focusing section, scientists were able to obtain precise beam trajectory measurements with a level of accuracy at 1 millimeter, as demonstrated in the analysis of AWAKE Run 2 data.  Additionally, researchers were able to accurately measure the electron beam's trajectory at a range of plasma densities from 3.8 to 7.2*10^14 cm^-3.  This method has been found to be applicable across various plasma stages and is deemed to be a reliable option for future experiments.

This study addresses local differential privacy in distributed decision tree learning through development of multiple algorithms to guarantee privacy for individual data points, including algorithms for guaranteed-privacy generation and merging of encoded data. Furthermore, several evaluation methods are introduced to determine the differential privacy rate of resulting data sets. Utilizing theoretical analysis and empirical testing, the study shows that a proposed approach to privately learning decision trees via a histogram-based data encoding method meets the requirements for both local and differential privacy, offering a combination of privacy-guaranteed data encoding and aggregation methods. As a result, this study's methods exhibit comparable accuracy to non-private approaches while maintaining data privacy, outperforming previous methods in terms of accuracy with similar privacy settings. The methods are particularly suited for large-scale distributed learning scenarios due to their efficient computation time. The study's source code is available on GitHub under the project name private-decision-tree.

We introduce a family of regularized entropy-regularized optimal transport problems, where a Bregman divergence is used instead of the traditional Wasserstein distance in optimal transport theory. This includes a specific instance where our model simplifies to the Laplacian regularized optimal transport, particularly relevant in the context of physics. To solve these new optimization problems, we develop a proximal gradient method that is guaranteed to converge monotonically, and provide numerical examples to demonstrate its effectiveness, including an application to the speed-up of neural network training in high dimensions.

This paper introduces a novel approach for advancing discrete dynamic Bayesian networks, chain event graphs, and hidden Markov models using a Bayesian maximum a posteriori framework. It proposes a dynamic selection method for model components, enabling the integration of multiple models and efficient detection of the best-fit model in time series data. This approach builds on the fundamental principle of integration, allowing for the simultaneous analysis of numerous models, resulting in the automatically selected best model as a byproduct of processing the data. The method's performance is demonstrated using simulated and real-world data, including an in-depth analysis of a classic psychology study.

This research explores the convergence rates of the minimum norm solution in a broad class of regularization parameter update rules, applying second-order dynamics with no Tikhonov regularization, under convex objective and smooth, strongly convex, and strongly smooth constraint conditions. We find that the error rates in this scenario are significantly improved when compared to first-order dynamics, achieving optimal convergence rates of O(1/t) for strong convex and smooth constraint cases, along with a logarithmic factor for strong smooth constraint cases, thus yielding a significant acceleration. We also demonstrate that the error rates are strongly asymptotic in nature, requiring a sufficient time period of t > C/C^2, where C is a bound on the constraint condition number. We also establish a new bound on the error rates for path-following dynamics with no Tikhonov regularization and provide numerical examples that validate and extend our theoretical findings.

Following walls is a fundamental capability for robots, utilized across numerous applications and conditions. The unstable behavior of robots following walls is a problem that needs to be addressed, particularly since small fluctuations can lead to uncontrolled movements. The unsupervised learning approach has revealed 'unruly behaviors' in robots following walls, characterized by periodic and unpredictable movements, which were unexpected features. The number of turns a robot makes while following the wall not only fluctuates, but these fluctuations also increase exponentially, resulting in unpredictable movements. By analyzing these behaviors, it has been found that certain policies can produce more accurate results by incorporating 'unruly turns' into their models, leading to an increased robustness against uncertain environments.

Within the framework of a kinetic energy driven superconducting mechanism, where the coupling between conduction bands and charge reservoirs plays a crucial role, the authors investigate how it affects the response to electromagnetic radiation in superconductors with long-lasting penetration depth. The results show that the penetration depth exhibits significant temperature and frequency dependence, and these behavior persists across the superconducting regime. The authors further analyzed how it's affected by dopant location and concentration for the case of planar boundaries. The study reveals that planar boundaries with the boundary becoming fully neutralized display distinct features in their response to electromagnetic radiation, and such features disappear with further increases in doping levels. The study also shows that planar boundaries with large doping levels exhibit frequency-independent behavior, and the study suggests that such behavior can be utilized to identify and study extended defects that run perpendicular to the surface, as their appearance is associated with distinct features in the penetration depth at low frequencies that increase with frequency. The study demonstrates that perpendicular to surface defects exhibit distinct behavior that increase with frequency. The study also shows that such behavior can be utilized to identify and study the effects induced by the interaction between long-lived excitations and the coupling between the conduction band and the charge reservoir. The study provides a comprehensive understanding of the long-lived behavior of superconductors that are mediated by the coupling between the conduction band and the charge reservoir.
