This research targets the advancement of common sense knowledge representation and processing capabilities. Current AI systems have achieved impressive performance in specific tasks such as vision and language modeling, but often fail to incorporate common sense elements in their decision-making processes. To address this, a significant update has been made to the COMET knowledge base, expanding from 15 to over 50 million relation facts, specifically tailored for natural language processing purposes. The accompanying dataset, COMET-ATOMIC 2020, is comprised of 32 high-level relation categories, encompassing 151 sub-categories, and is characterized by symmetric relationships. The proposed dataset provides an extensive resource for evaluating and developing both symbolic and statistical methods for AI systems. The authors also showcased state-of-the-art performance by neural network techniques in relation classification, and demonstrated the efficacy of graph embedding methods for generating common sense-driven dialogue using COMET-ATOMIC 2020.

The development of highly sensitive and robust interferometric telescope arrays, such as the Atacama Large Array to observe the Millimeter sub/mega galaxy, has enabled scientists to collect vast amounts of data, including numerous astronomical maps, although not yet fully exploited due to data reduction limitations. The researchers created the Hi-GAL Information Reduction Pipeline (IRP) to analyze data from the Herschel satellite's Guaranteed Time Domain, consisting of 67 blind scan maps, and evaluated its performance using comprehensive flags for data quality and cross-checking among different frequency bands. The IRP's final stage incorporates sophisticated image processing techniques, including an analysis of data reliability using calibrated uncertainty flags and an analysis of data variability across different maps, resulting in the production of high-quality, homogeneous images, accompanied by precise flux measurements, in the form of FITS files including flagged maps and uncertainty information.

A recent large-scale study using Gaia, VVV, and 2MASS data measured the chemical composition of older initial population stars in four globular clusters - 47 Tuc, omega Centauri, NGC 2808, and NGC 4833. This research particularly focused on NGC 2808, a rich Milky Way cluster, to verify the variation in metal content within the cluster, as earlier studies suggested. Our analysis of NGC 2808's 68 red giant stars, with metal content ranging from -0.2 to -0.9, was conducted using spectra covering three specific regions. Our findings, along with iron content levels, were calculated based on the Abundance Matching algorithm, resulting in iron abundance precision of less than 0.2 dex, iron to oxygen ratio precision of less than 0.3, and iron abundance standard deviation precision of less than 0.1 dex, as indicated by multiple star groups. Our metal content findings matched previous studies, as we detected two distinct metal populations within NGC 2808, indicating higher metal content population B had higher iron content levels, as compared to metal content population A, and both metal content populations had distinct iron to oxygen ratios, indicating variation. Our metal content analysis further confirmed metal content population A had lower iron content levels, as compared to metal content population B, and both metal content populations had distinct iron content ranges, indicating wider metal content populations had distinct iron content ranges, indicating variation. Analysis of duration and frequency for initial exit events in two-dimensional single file diffusions is carried out. Using a reference point based approach, we develop expressions for mean and variance of exit duration within single file diffusions when the starting area is a broad range of convex shapes. We also compare theoretical findings with corresponding numerical results, showcasing good agreement between theory and simulation. Furthermore, we find the mean exit duration exhibits an arrhenius temperature dependence. It is found that the temperature variation in the mean exit duration can provide information about the interior and boundary parameters of the diffusion process. Moreover, we observe that the mean exit duration decreases as the interior of the region being analyzed becomes larger while keeping the boundary fixed in size, indicating that the mean exit duration is influenced by the arrhenius temperature dependence of the interior and boundary parameters. In addition, frequency analysis of initial exit events reveals that the variance of duration frequency generally scales as the square of mean duration, providing evidence of a stationary renewal process in the two-dimensional single file diffusions.

Quantum Bayes' Theorem has been widely utilized in various scientific areas for drawing out hidden patterns and relationships by iteratively updating probabilities based on new discoveries. In physics, this method plays a crucial role in numerous applications ranging from cosmology to medical imaging using PET scans. The aim of this paper is to validate the relevance and utility of Quantum Bayes' Theorem in understanding how scientists derive conclusions when performing measurements in quantum physics. The paper begins by reviewing the underlying principles of Quantum Bayes' Theorem and applying them to a simple yet essential scenario in quantum physics, namely, two particles emitting polarized photons. The paper then tackles a controversy over whether quantum physics can reliably indicate causality in the case of particle polarization anisotropy, and it shows through its analysis that Quantum Bayes' Theorem affirms the consistency of drawing conclusions based on quantum physics principles, including the principles of wave function collapse and entanglement. The paper concludes by discussing its general findings how Quantum Bayes' Theorem consistently upholds the principles of quantum physics as a non-anomalous framework in understanding the world.

The established QCD equation of state within the temperature-chiral condensate plane has been questioned, with certain researchers suggesting its validity only at "moderate" temperatures. In this context, we demonstrate the sQCD equation of state's, and thermal pressure's, theoretical foundations, using QCD sum rules in models with a temperature of up to $2\,T_{c}$. These properties are analogous to those found in the QCD equation of state. We also derive the chromodynamic gas equation of state, and demonstrate that at $1.2\,T_{c}$ the quark condensate's thermal expansion behavior mirrors that of a relativistic hadron gas, with similar behavior observed for the SU(2) symmetric phase's thermal pressure. Notably, we reveal that beyond $1.5\,T_{c}$ the quark condensate's thermal expansion behavior diverges from that of a relativistic hadron gas, with a similar divergence observed in its pressure. In an effort to clarify, we establish four distinct hadron gas equation of state benchmarks, evaluating the compatibility of these hadronic models with the QCD equation of state.

The Steenrod algebra's cohomology groups are significant in studying permutation orbits of points in irreducible representations of the symmetric group. However, there's a common misconception that cohomology's based on the Steenrod algebra is simply an ignorable phenomenon. In reality, this notion is clearly false. In fact, there are specific key elements within key cohomology groups that are indeed significant and crucial to the study of permutation orbits. These key elements are often characterized by the Steenrod square's action. Furthermore, there are some key foreign insertion operations whose actions on cohomology can be easily combined with the Steenrod square's. In contrast, other cohomology elements are generated by ignorable insertion operations such as the reverse Schur insertion. This separability implies that ignorable insertions only affect a negligible portion of cohomology. This insight can be utilized in avoiding ignorable cohomology when computing permutation orbits, thus speeding up computation. Specifically, this can be seen in computing orbits of points in representations where the code for the permutation is isomorphic to a Young subgroup of the symmetric group.

A new optical Lyman-alpha filter is being developed for ground-based astronomical applications, offering high precision and stability. This filter, designed to a specific wavelength and frequency, can enable photometric measurements in the Lyman ultraviolet region, currently limited due to atmospheric distortion. The model incorporates specifications from the Kepler telescope's Lyman-alpha filter, proposed for the Kepler-4 instrument on the Kepler-4 telescope. The proposed filter is designed to a precision of 0.01 mag, and its development involves characterizing various optical components to ensure the achieved precision. An independent Lyman-alpha filter model is also presented for independent use, and the paper provides detailed information on the filter's specifications, and demonstrates their applicability through example calculations, including mock bandpasses, and their use in the Kepler-4 telescope's photometry mode.

Ideal controllers for network systems have unique properties, including an implicit influence on local data and the ability to independently operate node functions, while also limiting communication between nodes to information exchanges along the graph's spectral contours. However, their widespread application in complex networks is hindered by complex computation and stringent data transmission constraints. This study introduces a novel, distributed algorithm for computing ideal controllers via graph filter operations. It is demonstrated that an appropriate graph filter, along with a communication scheme between nodes, enables a collaborative summation of local data, yielding an accurate estimate of the ideal controller. This method is versatile, allowing the proposed algorithm to function even in the presence of noisy conditions, while its summation bandwidth can be dynamically adjusted for optimized performance. Numerical simulations are conducted to verify the efficacy of this method, showcasing its potential for streamlined computation and data transmission. This study sets the stage for a range of applications of ideal controllers in graph signal processing.

A novel technique for automatically categorizing images based on their visual content has been developed, utilizing an unsupervised indexing method that accommodates dynamic updates. Although images are typically represented by fixed-length vectors, they are subject to changes due to various factors, resulting in inaccurate and unstable predictions. In response, a probabilistic framework for image classification has been designed. By simulating the performance of a neural network using Monte Carlo sampling and various perturbation methods, the accuracy of image predictions can be assessed in a probabilistic format. This enables an image dataset to be indexed with confidence thresholds, allowing for the specification of a minimal level of reliability. In addition, the indexing dataset can be dynamically updated by re-indexing images that exhibit high confidence levels, thereby ensuring the maintenance of optimal performance. This categorization system, now known as Dynamic Picture Indexing (DPI), has been thoroughly tested using diverse datasets, encompassing datasets of car models (GQAcar), fine-art paintings (Artist Portraits), street scene images (Scene Underwear), traffic videos (TUS), and fashion garments (YMM). In each case, the indexing system has successfully identified images that could serve as representative samples for their respective classes, thereby facilitating dynamic updates without a need for supervision. All datasets, along with the corresponding code, can be accessed at https://github.com/GeorgianTechCS237/DPI.

This study verifies the existence of a blind key generation process through local randomness extraction in memoryless, discrete, and inseparable sources over Gaussian channels. A binary source with independent values has been analyzed, and an lower bound on the key generation rate has been formulated in terms of the source's entropy, its covariance matrix, and the transmission channel characteristics. Further, an algorithm based on a binary entropy function has been proposed to calculate a random variable from the source data, resulting in a verified lower bound on the key generation rate equal to the source entropy. Consequently, this implies that a blind key generation rate not exceeding the source entropy is feasible. In the special case of a source value set of size $2^N$, this implies that a key can be generated from that set size, resulting in a blind key generation rate not exceeding its entropy. In the binary symmetric source with error probability $\epsilon$ for size $2^{nR}$ transmitted over a binary symmetric channel, this implies that a blind key generation rate not exceeding $1 - nR - \frac{3}{4}\epsilon^2n$ is achievable for all $\epsilon <.475$. Washboard-like energies occur frequently in research, particularly in solid-state devices, but a long-standing issue has hindered analysis - the absence of a proximal analytical structure. A key feature of these energies is that they display uniform transport characteristics, which we utilize to develop a dynamic model, initially in one dimension and then extendable to higher dimensions. Our work also examines the washboard energy in the context of stochastic dynamics, with the goal of identifying the conditions under which drift and diffusion coefficients are finite. Finally, we apply our theoretical results to evaluate the washboard energy in detailed balance with a delta-correlated white noise and compare them with numerical simulations.

This research introduces an enhanced version of the Kim (1998) non-random sampling algorithm, designed to determine impulse response functions from a diverse range of economic datasets, including non-randomly sampled datasets, differently timed datasets, and datasets containing varying degrees of noise. The algorithm's initial iteration utilizes a Kim (1998) type weighted average to calculate the local projection. Thereafter, it iteratively applies a nonlinear programming algorithm, using a Loss Function that calculates the optimal weights for minimizing the difference between estimated and actual impulse response functions. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, the algorithm has been validated on generated macro-econometric impulse response series. Additionally, the algorithm has been successfully applied to calculate the impulse response functions of a GARCH-based model, a GARCH-RCVAE model, and real-world data from the NBER's Pharmaceutical Database.

A classical particle with positive or negative charge placed in a magnetic field develops an inherent angular momentum due to its interaction with the field. This property is based on the angular momentum distribution of the quantum vacuum itself. The magnitude of the angular momentum transferred from the vacuum to the charged particle depends on the charge of the particle, its radius, and the intensity of the magnetic field. Specifically, a particle with an electric charge q attached to a solenoidal magnetic field experiences an angular momentum of (q^2 * B)/2, measured in units of J*z, which is equivalent to (q^2*B*z)/h. This value can be translated to an angular momentum of (q*B*z)/h, which corresponds to an electron spin. This inherent angular momentum of the quantum vacuum also applies to particles with half-integer spin and charges governed by non-Abelian gauge theories.

This study introduces a new dataset, FGNET-RH, which builds on the existing FGNET dataset by including hierarchical information to enhance the disambiguation process for names. The research also explores the efficacy of using hyperbolic neural network models, particularly for refining and improving entity classification outcomes, given the dataset's complex hierarchical structure. The results of the experiments, which included comparisons with alternative models and the original FGNET dataset, indicated that the FGNET-RH dataset maintains consistency with expert-annotated data and demonstrates superior performance in entity classification compared to a baseline model. The FGNET-RH dataset is now accessible through this link: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1Qs0T2sP6z0QsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQsQ

We express the Hankel determinants for the second form as iterated integrals of the real functions associated with starlike functions of order $\beta$. This helps establish exact expressions, connections to the radius of convexity, and lower bounds for the determinants. Moreover, we obtain specific values for the determinants within the classes $\mathcal{U}$ and $\mathcal{S}$.

To address the issue of unpredictable future demand for virtual resources in a cloud computing environment, advanced load management techniques are employed to make informed decisions about allocating virtual components. A proposed strategy, called Prepartition, involves predicting future demands and reserving virtual resources accordingly. Due to the unpredictability of demands and limitations of virtual components, precise reservations often result in excessive resource waste, motivating the search for an optimal solution. A novel approach, called Prepartition, combines predictive modeling and resource reservation to minimize waste. By modeling the virtual population on a unit interval and applying non-decreasing, concave functions, Prepartition achieves near-optimal results. Simulation results indicate that this method leads to reduced over-provisioning and subsequent waste compared to traditional methods.

The objective of this study is to develop AI systems capable of anticipating how multiple autonomous agents, programmed with different decision-making methodologies, will reach a state of equilibrium. Given that certain agent behaviors are influenced by learned parameters, the paper focuses on finding a way for the AI system to learn and anticipate the equilibrium alongside these parameters. It introduces an innovative architecture called Fixed Point Networks, where the AI system's task is divided into two parts: one for evaluating how different parameters impact equilibria and another for determining which parameters are necessary. The study presents theoretical justification for the feasibility of this architecture and conducts experiments to demonstrate its effectiveness using both simple theoretical models and a complex game scenario.

In finding out cause-and-effect relationships between multiple variables, we develop new methods that work effectively, are efficient, and accurately identify relationships even when there's noise. These new methods, which we've adapted for complex data sets, are based on previous research and focus on the specific connections it's possible to identify. To demonstrate the value of these new methods, we use them to analyze how different factors are related, even when there's no initial cause, in order to better understand cause-and-effect relationships. Furthermore, we develop a method that allows us to identify specific connections, even when dealing with large numbers of variables and variables with missing information, and we show its accuracy by testing it using generated data sets. To demonstrate its value, we use this method to analyze how different factors are connected in a study of social media, even when dealing with extensive data sets.

We're developing an efficient monitoring system for LTI systems under covert attacks. The framework combines an offline linear model and an online nonlinear classifier. The offline model is created by solving a convex optimization problem that estimates the system's normal behavior based on historical data. The online non-linear classifier utilizes an ANOM detection method with nonlinear mappings to detect stealthy attacks in real-time. The effectiveness of the proposed framework was tested on a nonlinear missile and linear power grid models. The results show that the framework provides accurate detection without system disruption and reliable performance over time.

A precise summary condenses a lengthy document into a clear, concise outline, still capturing its primary insights. Current tools mainly cater to English speakers, leaving Indian language speakers largely ignored. This paper proposes a dual pathway summurization framework, evaluating the effectiveness of both text and graph-based summurization using GAE-ISumm, a GAN-based approach. Experimental results across four major Indian languages - Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, and Marathi - demonstrate the superiority of GAE-ISumm over other summurization frameworks, with a particularly notable performance in graph-based summurization that outperforms the state-of-the-art on English.

We introduce the concept of S-rings of the Noetherian type, distinct from standard rings, and carry out classification for the specific case of finitely generated algebras over a field of the characteristic zero, analogous to the classification of Noetherian rings. Additionally, some previously known results regarding standard material in characteristic zero are reevaluated in this context, along with the identification of new counterexamples in the treatment of join closures in Noetherian S-rings.

The discovery rate of transiting exoplanets is increasing rapidly thanks to automated analysis techniques, and these discoveries are being made in large numbers among nearby stars. Unfortunately, the complexity of analyzing the radial velocity variations of nearby stars is still largely undertaken manually. By combining the radial velocity data with the findings of the HADES project, which has identified a significant number of accelerating stars, this study demonstrates the value of incorporating these stars into the study of exoplanetary science. By examining a sample of 34 stars from the HADES project, this research establishes constraints on the masses and distances of unseen companions that influence the star's motion by means of astrometry. By applying a sophisticated analytical model, this study is able to account for the companion's effect on the star's motion in three dimensions, revealing a significant number of cases where there is clear evidence for a massive companion, and providing valuable constraints on the properties of others. The study's findings include constraints on massive companions ranging in size from Jupiter to the size of Uranus, which are found near or exceed the limits imposed by their proximity to the star. Notably, one system (HIP 11393) is found to contain a massive (4.5 M Jupiter) companion that orbits close to the star (0.20 AU) within the star's habitable zone, and (least of all) a nearby (20 AU) companion (0.23 M Jupiter) influenced by a third unseen companion.

Deep disentanglement using variational Bayesian autoencoders holds promise for uncovering underlying patterns within unsupervised time-series data, but the problem is largely understudied. We introduce a minimal approach by combining a straightforward Gaussian encoder and decoder with parameter tying, resulting in the lightweight bVAE model. Despite its simplicity, bVAE surpasses the performance of the standard, fully flexible vBA model across various datasets. We observed that the success of the bVAE model can be attributed to several regularization effects stemming from its simplified architecture. Additionally, the model's performance can be further enhanced by incorporating additional regularization techniques such as early stopping, which can help prevent overfitting, while other regularization techniques like dropout tend to compromise the model's ability to capture underlying patterns.

This paper outlines a novel sensor network designed to enhance customer experience by leveraging IoT systems to optimize intelligent home living. We develop an integrated system utilizing a private blockchain and GPS technology to support efficient data processing and enhance user experience. The proposed method incorporates machine learning algorithms, specifically K-means clustering, to accurately locate GPS and sensor data collection points inside a building, thus enhancing the efficiency of computation and data transfer. The system incorporates a blockchain-based service cache to expedite desired information retrieval. Furthermore, a localization technique using GPS, Wi-Fi, and sensor data is developed to determine a user's position. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, demonstrating its ability to process GPS and sensor data efficiently and accurately locate a user's position within an indoor setting.

A widely used still-image compression technique, difference modulation (DM), has the advantage of offering processing flexibility by operating outside of the modulation classifier, which can be computationally intensive. Its method of quantizing l-value information through thresholding results in either too coarse or overly expensive quantization, which can lead to reduced compression ratio and decoding errors, respectively. To overcome this limitation, a novel approach called deep learning-based quantization of l-values (DLQ) is proposed for improved l-value communication. By replacing conventional thresholding with a learning-based technique, DLQ achieves better results than quantization and helps increase the compression ratio, ultimately resulting in greater signal detection accuracy and reduced decoding error, which translates to better overall performance. Using simulated data, our approach demonstrates superior performance to thresholding and fixed-point quantization methods.

Crowdsourced datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for classification tasks. This issue is particularly prominent in visual data analysis, where noisy labels can drastically impact the performance of machine learning models. This research proposes an innovative approach to addressing this problem, building on existing work in ensemble modeling. This method utilizes crowdsourced label data to create 'human softmax' distributions, which are then fed into an ensemble model to produce reliable output. This method leverages noisy data to improve the accuracy of clean data, effectively mitigating the detrimental effects of noisy labels. This research showcases the application of this approach to two crowdsourced datasets - the Airline Reviews dataset and the Yahoo! Mystery Hunt dataset. Both datasets demonstrate the efficacy of this method in ensemble modeling, which can also be applied to other datasets to improve model performance.

This study provides conditions that guarantee a transfer operator for a semiflow, which may have unstable components, remains a bounded or contraction mapping within a specific Banach space. The findings are illustrated by analyzing the transfer operators of one-dimensional and two-dimensional systems, which have been well-documented in the literature. The work also examines the spectral properties of transfer operators for multiflows using a novel approach.

This work focuses on the concept of covering arrays with strength two, where the goal is to minimize the array size based on the number of distinct elements. We introduce various ideas to reduce the size of such arrays, including new parameters known as generalized groupability and weak groupability. These parameters are connected to other well-established characteristics like subset coverability and blockability. Additionally, there are given examples of situations in which subset coverability and blockability are not interchangeable, as well as an example illustrating that there is no correlation between groupability and weak groupability. Furthermore, there is provided an algorithm for creating a covering array that leverages generalized groupability, and an examination of the relations between different parameters via a practical problem involving a tumor's blood supply.

One-way communication systems where one party sends multiple possible values and the other party uses an unknown function to select the correct one are considered weakly useful in the worst case, despite being able to correctly identify any given function with a high probability of success. In a two-party system where one party sends a value based on an unknown function and the other party uses an unknown transformation on the value and sends it back, it's known but not widely published that such systems where the function and transformation are closely linked are determinable. In a system where the function and transformation are not closely linked, such systems are essentially as useful as one-way systems in the worst case, and in a system where the function and transformation are not completely unknown but rather randomly chosen, such systems are not weakly useful in the worst case. In a system where the function and transformation are not closely linked and are freely chosen, such systems are not weakly useful in the worst case.

This study builds on and replicates the findings of a 2016 study that employed a guided genetic procedure to automatically generate crash-worthy web pages. Utilizing the same dataset and a comparable evaluation method, our replication seeks to confirm the original study's results, which revealed significant improvements in usability and web development efficiency compared to preceding studies. Key similarities between our replication and the original study include the use of the same dataset consisting of 50 WebCrawled data entries, the development of 10 automated web pages per entry via a guided genetic procedure, and the implementation of a controlled human evaluation to assess their performance. Additionally, our replication employs a blind, within-subjects trial to measure how users rank automated and human-generated web pages. Our replication efforts aimed to replicate all aspects of the original study, including its potential limitations.

The unusual "fisheyes" in vortices within high-temperature cuprate superconductors have long captivated the attention of researchers due to their intricate structures. Despite extensive research, the underlying causes for these intricate structures remain unclear in the commonly accepted theory of type-II superconductors. Our study provides direct visualization of the transition from an ordinary square lattice of vortex structures to a square-square lattice configuration in Nd1.85CuO4 (NCO) using a technique known as "Bitter bridges." By employing "Bitter bridges" to analyze vortices, we identified a previously unseen transition from an ordinary square lattice of vortex structures to a square-square lattice configuration, which was confirmed through careful analysis of the patterns observed. Our study also shows that this transition is caused by the splitting of individual vortex strings due to increased magnetic field, resulting in the formation of a complex square-square lattice structure, providing new insights into the mysterious "fisheyes" observed in other superconductors. The findings from our study offer a new perspective on the structure of vortex arrangements in materials with unusual properties.

Investigating thermal photons in high-energy proton-proton collisions using a specific method called directional flow analysis, researchers find that this phenomenon can be used to measure the viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma. Extending existing transport models to include thermal photons, researchers analyze their results and discover that as collision centrality increases, so does their directional flow. This suggests that the interaction between thermal photons and the dynamic medium is similar to those of hadrons. Based on this observation, researchers propose that the directional flow of thermal photons can be used to determine the shear viscosity to entropy density ratio of the medium, potentially leading to a more precise measurement.

We conduct a theoretical study to explore the Arrhenius behavior in an array of triangular and kagome structures supporting consistent magnetic arrangements. The kagome structure's uniform magnetic configuration, specifically with four spins per unit cell as a basic unit of analysis, displays an inherent self-similarity that extends to the triangular structure with three spins per unit cell, specifically with N=4 and with magnetic moments aligned either parallel or anti-parallel. This self-similarity relationship holds true for larger N values as well. A detailed transformation is established to show that for parallel moments, parallel and anti-parallel moments are equivalent in certain context, while for anti-parallel moments, they produce ferromagnetic, antiferromagnetic and spin glass-like interactions for certain context. This understanding is built based on the principle that large arrays of spins behave as continuous objects, thereby allowing mapping of magnetic moments as continuous vectors, thereby leading to a transfer of this understanding to analysis based on density matrices. A search for self-similar patterns in the time-evolution of spin-glass-like interactions through numerical simulation using Monte Carlo method is also performed, thereby revealing the presence of parallel and anti-parallel moments for a certain parameter value. The study also highlights a shift from a glass-like behavior to a glass-like behavior with increasing temperature. Upon analyzing temperature-dependent magnetic curves, a reversible shift from a glass-like behavior to a glass-like behavior with increasing temperature is observed. A search for the underlying cause for this shift is also performed

To boost efficiency in large-scale experiments, new methods have been developed that specifically identify intervention effects while controlling false discovery rates (FDR). The intervention effect is a critical outcome in various settings, yet current strategies often struggle with reliable performance when data is non-orthogonal or non-linear. To address these limitations, we have designed an innovative approach that leverages posterior probability thresholds to precisely identify intervention effects while regulating FDR. Our approach enhances conventional methods like the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure by utilizing thresholding for posterior probabilities, achieving controlled FDR and empirical performance improvements. Additionally, we have tailored our strategy for online applications where data arrives incrementally, accelerating computation and achieving better control of FDR. The effectiveness of our methods has been demonstrated through empirical analysis using the Pro/Classic dataset commonly employed in this field.

The universe's metric scale factor has been found to undergo exponential growth, which can be expressed as a power function of time, specifically $a(t) = t^p$, this way changing the equation of motion for a free falling object as described by the geodesic equation, this object will follow a straight line with constant acceleration in the accelerating universe, which will be interpreted as movement.

Using a novel approach to the type-X two Higgs doublet model, we have revisited the type-X 2HDM in light of the latest muon anomalous magnetic moment results. We found that its prediction for the $W$ boson mass is consistent with both the observed values of its mass and the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon. By analyzing constraints from the effective field theory approach, we determined that its FitzHauter parameter cannot exceed 0.2, and we found a type-X specific constraint of $\lambda_{\phi_1} \leq 0.4$. This model's performance emerges when considering the type-X role of $\phi_1$ in generating the Higgs vev and the $W$ mass, and when $\phi_2$ is primarily responsible for the difference between the $f_2$ mass and its invariant mass, resulting in additional constraints for the model's parameter space.

This research introduces SWIFTER, a technique for generating straightforward English descriptions of core mathematical concepts through interactive machine learning. For each pre-defined concept, the system gathers challenging natural language queries from users, selects the most difficult ones, and presents them to crowd workers for evaluation. Based on their input, the system refines the queries to create new, simplified versions, which are then ranked by relevance. The system combines these rephrased queries with concept names to train a model that generates concise, concept-specific definitions. This definition is then applied to provide answers for unknown queries regarding the concept. In contrast to prior research, the current framework differs in three key aspects: (1) it utilizes challenging queries from online directories, (2) includes crowd workers' input beyond label annotation, and (3) enables concept-specific definitions. The system's effectiveness was tested with concepts from the DBpedia and Wikidata databases, and after training on 1% of available queries, it successfully defined 57% of concepts accurately, showcasing promising performance. This research was conducted as a crowdsourced study, resulting in (375,000) human-computer interactions.

In the realm of representation learning, where a vast array of data is being generated at an unprecedented rate, there are numerous techniques being employed to create compact representations that can effectively capture the underlying structure of available data. These representations, in turn, facilitate a multitude of applications, including both supervised and unsupervised tasks, by utilizing different techniques such as classification, clustering, and anomaly detection. While effective in their respective domains, these methods are constrained by either requiring an abundance of labeled data or being limited to specific types of algorithms. However, a novel approach using neural networks offers an alternative pathway to representation learning by leveraging unsupervised learning and a highly flexible, layer-wise optimization process. This study seeks to explore the application of this neural network-based unsupervised learning approach, specifically a stacked variational autoencoder, to develop a novel metric for speech synchronization and asynchronous detection. Our proposed method is validated through a series of spoken dialogue tasks by analyzing speech from individuals with dysarthria and those without, leveraging a widely employed speech database known as the Jukebox Speech Database. Our analysis reveals notable accuracy and sensitivity rates, including 87.3% and 75.9% respectively, on a subset of speakers (n = 52), along with a range of 0.1930 to 0.2888 in classification and 0.5901 to 0.8100 in asymptotic sensitivity on an individual basis. The second iteration of the web-based application, RCSEDv2, has been released with a range of new features and enhancements. Building on the success of RCSEDv1, which facilitated data visualization for spectroscopic and imaging data, RCSEDv2 has expanded its capabilities to include elastic search functionality alongside improved plotting tools and streamlined data analysis. Featuring a user-friendly interface with preset options, RCSEDv2 allows for the creation of various data visualizations, including 2D, 3D, and spectral data, with integrated tools for spectrophotometry and photometry. In addition, RCSEDv2 includes a range of new features, including the ability to upload and share datasets, access a library of atmospheric models, and generate HTML5 animations for interactive data visualization. Available online at http://rcsed.vipce.com, RCSEDv2 represents a powerful platform for data analysis and dissemination within the astronomical community.

Temporal action segmentation, a crucial task in video understanding, entails 
identifying discrete, unique actions within video timelines. Most existing 
methods focus on learning pre-existing video datasets through trial-and-error. 
This paper presents a new, resilient technique that can be applied on various 
video sources with minimal reliance on prior knowledge or human annotation. 
Key innovations include a novel feature representation method called HuMap, a 
cluster-based approach to differentiate distinct actions, and an unsupervised 
action discovery algorithm that identifies distinct actions automatically. 
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel framework, 
as it achieves exceptional outcomes on STCTV, UCF101-24, and HMDB51 datasets, 
outperforming other approaches significantly, and producing results comparable 
to or surpassing state-of-the-art methods on Kinetics400, ActivityNet, and 
DGGNet. Additionally, comprehensive ablation studies reveal the crucial role 
of essential components within our proposed framework.

Through the present algebra, we investigate the existence of $\bar{K} D^{(*)}$, $\bar{K}^{*} D^{(*)}$, $\bar{K} \pi$, $\bar{K}^{*} \pi$ hidden-charm pentaquark states and create relevant pole residues. Utilizing the geometric scaling principle, we determine the energy parameters for these pentaquark states and estimate their widths by employing the Gautschi method and the in-medium regulatory factor $\Gamma_{\text{reg}}$. Consequently, we obtain the mass values of $M_{\bar{K}D} =  Vert 2.94 \pm 0. 15_{\text{stat}}i_{0. 15} ~\text{MeV}$, $M_{\bar{K}^{*}D} = Vert 2.84 \pm 0. 14_{\text{stat}}i_{0. 14} ~\text{MeV}$, $M_{\bar{K}D^{*}} = Vert 2.83 \pm 0. 14_{\text{stat}}i_{0. 14} ~\text{MeV}$, $M_{\bar{K}^{*}D^{*}} = Vert 2.74 \pm 0. 13_{\text{stat}}i_{0. 13} ~\

Conventional assessment methods used in software testing education fail to provide effective learning outcomes, as they tend to emphasize examination grades over practical skills development. This issue can be resolved by adopting a novel approach that focuses on learning goals, as proposed by the Assessment for Learning framework. The chosen goal type for this study is "developing", which aims to improve learners' abilities rather than merely replicating past work. The research compares two types of assessment methods: detailed reviews of projects and conceptual questions, with regards to their potential to help students grow and improve. An experiment was conducted with an introductory course consisting of 122 students, using both tools to assess their knowledge and skills over three rounds. The results show that conceptual questions are more effective in helping students develop and improve, as they are more likely to address "know-how" goals, receive feedback, and enhance their understanding of testing techniques, whereas project reviews focus mainly on "know-about" goals, although they receive feedback and demonstrate improved project skills. Overall, both assessment methods have their uses, with project reviews evaluating students' practical abilities and conceptual questions assessing their ability to think critically and learn effectively.

Domain adaptation has been used to develop more versatile models across various domains. However, existing approaches often rely on domain-relevant data which can be difficult and expensive to collect. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel method for adapting models without relying on such data. Instead, we utilize a source model trained on a related task, along with unlabeled target data. To achieve this, we develop a method to estimate target labels utilizing a target data distribution. Multiple neural network predictors are generated in an exploration process, with their predictions evaluated and top-performing predictors combined to generate refined labels for the target data. These refined labels are then utilized to adapt the source model to the target domain, resulting in improved performance on the target domain. Our approach outperforms other domain adaptation methods that do not rely on domain-specific data, and also compares favorably to other semi-supervised domain adaptation methods that utilize additional supervision.

The use of Gas Core Reactors in space offers several advantages, including high power outputs, efficient heat transfer, and the potential for nuclear explosions, making them suitable for various remote space applications such as satellites, lunar and planetary bases, and propulsion systems. This report provides an overview of GCR technology and its applications, followed by a discussion of the benefits and drawbacks of using GCRs in space environments. It also serves as an update to a 2019 report, with new sections focusing on propulsion systems and civilian space stations, in addition to discussions on recent progress in GCR research, updates on existing space projects, and concluding remarks, including recommendations for future development.

This study presents a novel neural network approach for particle physics research that utilizes a straightforward, interpretable design based on physical insights. A full-scale reanalysis of the highest-energy neutrino observed to date was conducted using the fully-trained models from a previous competition, where we focused solely on fine-tuning the network's parameters to optimize localization and energy predictions of neutrino interactions. By leveraging domain-specific insights, we were able to implement novel, domain-aware modules within the network's architecture that enhance its performance. This innovative approach achieved superior accuracy in neutrino energy reconstruction with a mean absolute error of 25%, as well as precise localization with average interquartile range values of 0.155 and 0.164 in x and y directions, respectively.

The EXOPLINES repository, hosted at http://exo.plines.io, is an extensive online collection of accurate and experimentally-verified absorption cross-section data for key atmospheric molecules relevant to giant exoplanets and Brown dwarfs. The database features essential species including H2O, CH4, NH3, NH4+, H3O+, and HCN, with data tailored for various temperatures - 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600 K - and wide range of pressures - 10^-7 to 10^3 bar. For each species, we integrate comprehensive datasets from multiple sources, making it easier to differentiate between high-pressure and low-pressure settings. By leveraging the Splatalogue database, we provide access to the latest data for 40 atmospheric molecules and species at 100 K, enabling seamless planning and preparation for complex instruments like the ALMA. As an example of its utility, we demonstrate the impact of pressure on the interaction between water molecules and its counterpart protonated ammonium, with the data showing a substantial variation in absorption cross-section (~3 orders of magnitude) when pressure changes from high to low settings for this particular species.

This paper explores the theoretical foundations of semantic grounding in Answer Set Programming. We introduce an evaluation measure called 'gives rise to', also referred to as 'gives-rise-to', to assess the relationship between multiple layers of grounded knowledge. We establish the 'gives-rise-to-transitivity' theorem, while examining the relationship between this new measure and existing semantics. Furthermore, we discuss how the 'gives-rise-to' measure can be applied to Answer Set Programming via abductive and inductive reasoning.

In any universal resource theory, initial access to a single resource must be sufficient to create any possible state. We demonstrate that in such theories, the set of states accessible through initial pure single-resource use can be defined by a single non-negative parameter, which controls the amount of resource utilized. This conclusion applies to all universal resource theories, regardless of whether they involve convex coefficients. Moreover, we define a specific subset of resource states that we term 'elementary,' which not only includes states accessible through initial pure single-resource use but also those generated through initial mixed single-resource access. We rectify a previously debatable assertion by showing that the set of elementary states is unique and characteristic of the resource structure across various notations and frameworks.

A multivariate statistical framework is proposed to identify outliers and determine central tendency for a dataset by analyzing its moment sequences. The approach is based on a polynomial identification algorithm that utilizes an iterative process to find the most consistent moment configuration, thereby eliminating anomalous data points. Theoretical justification and empirical bounds are established for the statistical error in estimating the polynomial. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to generate central tendency estimators for univariate and multivariate datasets, which are shown to be robust against anomalous data. The theoretical findings are corroborated by numerical examples and real-world data applications.

We analyze multivariate time series data with long tails, characteristics not adequately addressed by existing statistical models. A new class of non-stable distributions with heavy tails is introduced, and their corresponding probability density functions are derived for observations from multivariate time series. A model, known as the non-stable multivariate time series model, is developed to analyze the mean and variance of the probability density functions, and a single link function is proposed to incorporate additional information. To estimate model parameters, maximum likelihood and iterative methods are utilized. A graphical method for diagnostics and outlier detection is presented, as well as the calculation of the residual and its impact on inference. Additionally, asymptotic theory for hypothesis testing and confidence intervals is formulated, and simulations demonstrate improved performance in heavy-tailed distributions compared to the multivariate autoregressive model. Finally, the model is applied to real-world data with notable results.

A novel approach to constructing high-rate quantum error-correcting codes, compatible with conventional low-density parity-check decoding methods, is presented. This approach enables the use of efficient linear-time classical decoders on codes with repeated qubits, thus providing a feasible path to achieve both high error threshold and high error rate, particularly with 3D lattice structures.

A data monitoring network is defined as a set of locations where an individual can stay to track environmental changes, such as temperature variations. A "controlling set" is a group of locations that allow for the accurate tracking of differences between nearby spots. A set is considered "distance-r-controlling" if the distances between each point and every other point can be calculated using the network's connected nodes, up to a certain range (r). A novel method for selecting a controlling set, specifically for high-girth graphs like lattices and some tree structures, involves identifying a subset of nodes such that, using nearby nodes' distances, the network's shape can be accurately mapped within a certain radius (r). By analyzing certain tree structures, it was shown that a controlling set for these networks is at least the same size as the network's diameter. Furthermore, it was discovered that a controlling set for a certain type of tree structure is always at most the square root of the network's size, but this was not true for all types of graphs.

Theoretical models have shown that correlated systems featuring bound states at boundaries and edges can exhibit topological properties. Researchers have suggested that such states could also exist in random systems. However, these proposals have yet to be implemented in any random material models. Recent research provides a framework to incorporate disorder into complex material models by incorporating disorder into the Bloch Hamiltonian's higher-order topological components. This approach was used to create two models, one describing a 2D chiral topological insulator and the other a 3D topological insulator, both of which incorporate random materials. The models predict the existence of correlated bound states at edges and corners in these complex materials. The probability distributions of their low-energy disorder spectra were analyzed and compared to the theoretical predictions of Green's function calculations. The research's results accurately represented the theoretical expectations of the disorder-free models, confirming the proposed framework's validity and providing insights into the disorder-induced properties of complex materials.

To find the origin of dark matter, the CMS and ALICE experiments are searching for signatures of supersymmetric particles at various energy levels. Despite multiple analyses being conducted across multiple collision energies, no supersymmetric particles have been detected yet. Based on stop and gluino decay patterns and the masses of their corresponding light counterparts, predicted neutralino masses have been narrowed down. In a 2011 search at 130 TeV, CMS analyzed data from Alkalai particles decaying into W bosons and neutralinos. As a result, dark matter masses between 40 and 110 GeV were ruled out. Also, in a 2018 search at 137 TeV, ALICE examined data from B-mesons decaying into W bosons and neutralinos, thereby excluding neutralino masses between 25 and 75 GeV. In addition to these findings, recent stop decay analyses in CMS experiments have revealed that dark matter masses up to 300 GeV have been ruled out for LHC operation at 13 TeV. Furthermore, in a 2020 simulation at 14 TeV, CMS analyzed data from LHCb experiments on charmed meson decay into W bosons and neutralinos, thereby excluding neutralino masses between 25 and 75 GeV. As a result, these experimental studies collectively leave only a small window of dark matter masses between 25 and 75 GeV and masses above 110 GeV open to investigation. These experimental findings serve as a foundation

While deep learning models excel across various tasks, their output predictions lack clarity, making it difficult for humans to grasp their internal workings. To mitigate this issue, there is a growing need for neural network visualization techniques that enhance our understanding of how these models operate. Our research introduces a new method for visualizing neural networks called bright field visualization, which effectively displays learning representations in high-dimensional neural network layers using geometric techniques. This approach transforms complex neural network layers into 3D structures that accurately represent the underlying geometric concepts, demonstrating improved outcomes and more insightful annotations in real-world image classification tasks, including increased accuracy and detailed label correlations.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2021 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 measurements across 1288 pairs and 1177 targets. A significant discovery of this study includes identifying 59 novel pairs or subsystems among nearby dwarf stars, primarily, adding to our ongoing speckle program. Our speckle program aims to monitor orbital movements of binaries within the solar neighborhood, specifically, high-order hierarchies, Hipparcos pairs, and also assess 892 members of young moving groups and associations, of which we resolved 103 new pairs.

We investigate special cases of the "heavenly" chiral algebra system, focusing on scenarios where three or four chiral factors apply, which can be interpreted as either distinct units or interconnected as a single integrated system. Our analysis shows that, in the context of classical systems interpreted through the geometric interpretation framework proposed in [arXiv:2103.13459], the resulting actions derived from the "heavenly" structures exhibit a notable property known as colour-kinematics equivalence. Our work also reveals that quantum generalisations of these special cases maintain this equivalence-kinematics relationship, further connecting these findings to the concept of scattering amplitudes, which are widely believed to be stable across different energy levels. It is also demonstrated that solutions exist where the "heavenny" chiral algebra system, when quantised, not only remains coherent but also maintains its integrability in a coherent manner. However, the special case where four chiral factors apply remains unsolved in its quantised state. Our work further expands the scope of applications for the "heavenly" chiral algebra by showcasing its potential in the context of the geometric interpretation framework, which was previously known only in the context of generalised Yang-Mills theory.

A rare event called piston surges can be observed in the chromosphere, where the movement of shock waves creates periodic patterns of dark bands due to the absorption of light by the surges. Although typically seen close to the sun's equator, researchers have been unable to fully understand how these surges form. To address this knowledge gap, scientists have observed and analyzed an exceptionally strong piston surge triggered by a jet event, which was captured by the LOFAR solar instrument. This analysis enabled researchers to study the speed and behavior of the piston surges as they move through the sun's atmosphere, while also making important advancements in the simulation of these events and their impact on scientists' understanding of the sun's dynamics.

In light of the enhanced sensitivity provided by the Belle II experiment, we carry out a frequency analysis regarding the adherence of the general two Higgs doublet model to two observed irregularities - anomalies in the muon magnetic moment and lepton flavor universality - as well as to the SM prediction of f_{B_{s, d}}. We assess the model's likelihood of incorporating these irregularities and, concurrently, generating a compatible f_{B_{s, d}} measurement. Utilizing Bayesian statistics, we investigate observable quantities, including m_{A}, tan beta, and various branching fractions. Our study reveals that, under certain conditions, the model faces a substantial probability of around 86%, stemming from the muon anomalous magnetic moment issue. In a different scenario, the model faces a substantially lower probability of around 12%, which is attributed to compatibility issues with both lepton flavor universality and the quark sector.

The study of random whirlpool development over time is an area of focus in this research. We begin by establishing a framework for random differential equations based on an existing probabilistic approach, then derive specific functional equations that pertain to the dynamics of a system. Next, we introduce the notion of solution unification, allowing for the analysis of different types of solutions under a single definition. Additionally, we establish a version of ODE unification, enabling the study of solutions under this broader definition. Finally, we apply our method to the analysis of random whirlpool dynamics, characterized by the movement of a particle's position z as a function of time z = z(t) in three-dimensional space, subject to the influence of a randomly changing downward-acting force represented by the function z''(t).

The state vector of a boson sampling process can be precisely written down using Szyger's formula, making it one of the few instances where the complete quantum system state is understood. Despite this achievement, analyzing the entire state vector doesn't offer any significant advantages in explaining the mysterious quantum phenomena occurring within it. The entire state vector's properties are explored for systems containing an even or odd number of bosons interacting with any number of modes. By employing a representation based on nonnegative orthogonal eigenstates, a description is given for the entire state vector's structure in terms of norm-constrained Hilbert space. Evidence suggests that these eigenstates are nonlocal entangled for small system sizes, heavily entangled multi-mode states, and single-site projected entangled states. Consequently, a very efficient method for detecting local entanglement in bipartite systems is developed, along with conjectured local unitary invariance, the entire state vector's entire multi-mode type entanglement entropy, and Renyi-2 entropy solutions.

Deep learning has significantly impacted the analysis of life science images and text, but its application in life science temporal sequence prediction remains limited due to memory constraints. Recent developments in temporal sequence prediction have improved but often rely on comprehensive training datasets, making it challenging to apply these methods to predictive tasks such as identifying protease cleavage sites based on protein structures. To address these limitations, we introduce a guided learning approach that uses a multi-stage training strategy to learn from sparse, high-dimensional data efficiently. Our proposed method allows us to predict temporal sequences of varying lengths, making it suitable for life science assessments where accurate predictions decrease in importance with distance from the focus point. Our approach outperforms other methods such as CNN and Transformers in protease cleavage prediction and protein contact angle prediction. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method in other life science prediction tasks such as predicting protein structures, identifying chemotaxis, and predicting protein-ligand binding energies.

In a series of pioneering works, covering more than four decades, Richard Bellman pioneered the application of dynamic programming to model real-time decision-making processes. His foundational book, "Strong Inference: Criteria for Accepting Data in Economics," further emphasized the importance of scientific methodology in economics. The decision-making framework he proposed involves three key components: a decision-maker, a plan, and a sequence of time steps. At each time step, the decision-maker generates a policy, executes an action based on that policy, perceives the outcome, and updates their understanding of the situation through a process called "beliefs." In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) employ a similar structure, consisting of a recursive model that allows for iterative decision-making, although the terms "policy" and "belons" are not commonly used in the context of RNNs. Building on Bellman's work, we explore the connections and potential collaborations between the fields of machine learning and the broader decision-making theory.

Current state-of-the-art action detection methods heavily rely on well-defined context, obtained through expensive cage-based annotation, to guarantee precise spatial attention for recognizing human actions.  However, this approach proves to be impractical for producing high-quality vision datasets due to the labor intensity of cage-based annotation.  To overcome this challenge, we introduce a novel self-supervised AutoContext model that dynamically learns context from video sequences without requiring explicit annotation.  Our method, specifically tailored for arbitrary video-based attention tasks, achieves performance on par with fully-supervised methods in our experimental evaluations on HOLISTIC and UAV-dataset.  Graph Convolutional Networks are leveraged to develop context for video sequences, allowing the model to learn context for video segments on a per-frame basis using spatial and temporal relationships between objects.  Our method also employs a novel self-supervised object query mechanism to identify critical objects within video sequences, where object identity is inferred by modeling interactions between objects, as revealed by temporal feature analysis.

A recent competition known as the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge brought together researchers to tackle the issue of identifying and understanding image similarity. This involved multiple tracks, including one focused on detecting copied content, and another focused on discovering new categories of similar images. The challenge featured state-of-the-art training datasets, and drew the participation of over 707 individuals, resulting in numerous submissions that demonstrated significant improvements over previous best approaches. In this article, we first discuss the outcome of the challenge, including the winning results. Next, we highlight some of the key discoveries and insights gained from the challenge. Finally, we explore the potential applications and advancements that may arise from the discovered knowledge.

This work focuses on examining singularities in parabolic equations resulting from various phenomena, including degeneration, boundary processes, and stability issues, using both qualitative and quantitative methods. It particularly investigates the development of regularity theories for degenerate boundary equations and singularities arising from them. Furthermore, an internal metastable phenomenon is analyzed, along with an overview of recent advances in homogenization theory.

This research aimed to examine the effect of a strong magnetic field on the energy distribution within a nucleus containing two particles. The study utilized the Local Spin Density Mean Spherical Approximation model in conjunction with the Local Coupled Variational method to obtain the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of the two-body Hamiltonian. The results showed that strong magnetic fields can impact the nucleus's energy spectrum. The study also revealed that symmetry breaking in the Hamiltonian's time-dependent component generates odd parity solutions for energies that are otherwise even. The research demonstrated that an additional effect of the strong magnetic field is to split energy levels of particles with $l=0$ into two distinct levels.

A successful approach to distributed training, Recursive Averaging (REC) minimizes communication overhead. We present a secure version of REC called DP-REC that handles sensitive data in a unified framework. DP-REC converts horizontal federated learning models into vertical models to utilize secure ensemble learning's compression benefits. The DP-REC protocol for stochastic REC requires only two secure multiparty operations: an additional computation, is demonstrated. We evaluate DP-REC's efficacy with real-world datasets and compare it to existing approaches, including a DP-based compression method, showing substantial improvements in communication efficiency while keeping data private.

A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus region has been constructed using GALEX's near-ultrtraviolet scan data, which have been cross-correlated with far-ultraviolet images. This correlation identified 61 heavily reddened background stars, the brightest of which has an estimated R_v of 2.35 and A_V of 24.5 magnitudes, located at approximately 140 parsecs or at the edge of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex. The color temperature of the scattering region is around 10,500 K for 23 of the stars and 13,000 K for the remaining 38, indicating the influence of young stars and ionizing sources. This is further supported by the detection of a far-ultraviolet excess 1.5 degrees west of LkH 2A, which has an estimated YSO energy output of 10 to 100 times L_o. The energy output corresponds to R_v = 3.5 and A_V = 5.6 magnes, roughly 20 to 40 times that of the LkH 2A's 1.5 k_o, which suggests LkH 2A no longer provides the region's primary energy source. Three other areas of similar YSO energy output have been found, one near LkH 2C, LkH 2D, and LkH 2A,

Document analysis is crucial for extracting insights from vast amounts of documents, 
which is a complex task due to varied document layouts and the multitude of languages used.
A feasible approach is to utilise structured analysis techniques on table-rich documents, 
enabling the rapid identification, prediction, and data extraction of tables.
Given the sequential nature of PDFs and tables, previous methods have employed graph neural networks 
for tabulation extraction, which we further develop by integrating PDF page image abstractions 
and layout configurations into graph nodes.
We also propose augmenting graph nodes with region-based vision models for further refinement, 
coupled with a page-level prediction model that leverages these enhanced graph nodes to produce outstanding results, 
which outperform state-of-the-art baselines with a recall-precision F1 score of 83.12 and 81.43 respectively, 
on the respective TAL table extraction dataset.

Focusing on complex, multi-stage decision-making processes with limited information, our model draws on the principles of hierarchical cognitive systems as the basis for player interaction. Building upon an existing theory by Sun, our research develops a new mathematical approach to represent cognitive levels in strategic decision-making processes. Additionally, our work incorporates concepts from epistemic theory to describe uncertainty and information transfer between players. As illustrative applications, our analysis examines cognitive dynamics in two-key coordination games, including the Prisoner's Dilemma and the Coordination game.

Population research has heightened the threat of the COVID-19 pandemic, prompting the development of multiple methods for estimating population densities from moving vehicle surveys.  The rapid progression of autonomous vehicle technology has inspired a new set of applications, with an increased emphasis on the social implications, given their potential to improve and augment human capabilities in challenging environmental conditions.  This research demonstrates the practicality of combining yaw rate and lateral acceleration sensors in low-cost automotive hardware to track target subjects, then applies these findings to population research in Mozambique, yielding significant enhancements in estimation accuracy across multiple assessment sites.  The results reveal more than a tenfold improvement in estimation accuracy when using the proposed method, compared to previous studies, with an associated reduction of at least 84% in required data collection efforts, thereby making the surveillance process significantly more sustainable and feasible.

The primary objective of an estimated filter is to determine an object's collection membership with a specified probability of error, using probabilistic queries to collection members.  Initially developed as a probabilistic counterpart to classic hash functions, filters like these have been applied in a wide range of applications, including testing for malware and detecting data corruption.  In this paper, we explore the possible utilization of filter ensembles in reducing the required collection storage space by decreasing the false positive rate.  Specifically, we investigate the requirements and properties as well as the performance of filter ensembles composed of randomly selected, regular $d$-variate filters.  We find that, for an object of fixed unknown membership, the probability of misidentifying a query as a member of a sufficiently large collection is close to $\exp(-\frac{kd\delta^2}{4})$, where $k$ is the number of filters within the ensemble, $d$ is the variable space dimension, and $\delta$ is the error probability.  We also find that, for an object of fixed known non-membership, the probability of misidentifying a query as a non-member is close to $\exp(-\frac{kpd^2\delta^2}{2})$, where $k$ is the number of filters within the ensemble, $d$ is the variable space dimension, $\delta$ is the error probability, and $p$ is the fraction of the collection that is comprised of members.

The theoretical basis for a multi-scale SPH method has been established, which aims to simulate complex multi-phase flows interacting with deformable objects and incorporate large eddy simulations. By preserving mass and momentum at each scale, as well as meeting a continuity condition, this approach simulates fluid behavior based on Lagrangian dynamics. A general formula for determining viscosity at the large eddy simulation level has also been derived. To transfer information between different scales, specific sparse interpolation matrices are used. A growing database that categorizes cells into different scales allows for dynamic adjustment of the approach's multi-scale configuration. To validate this method, simulations of various multi-phase fluid-structure interactions have been performed and the results have shown significant improvement in comparison to single-scale simulations, particularly in meeting physical principles and reducing transient effects. Moreover, the multi-scale approach has facilitated the simulation of multi-phase flows with reduced turbulent artificial viscosity, thereby allowing for more accurate representations of turbulent regimes. Ultimately, the multi-scale SPH framework has demonstrated its potential for efficient simulation of a wide range of scientific and engineering problems.

A recent application of Neural Network-based Vocoder techniques has shown that they can be used to modify the pitch of speech without affecting its tone, suggesting potential in speech synthesis. However, the initial speech synthesis models had limitations in their ability to change pitch without disrupting the speech quality. A pre-trained FastPitch model was used in this study to develop an algorithm that enhances pitch control while preserving the speech tone. The results indicate that this algorithm can effectively change pitch across a wide range of frequencies, both individually and in combination with other voice modifications, without negatively affecting the speech quality.

This research focuses on solving the (Temporal) Motif Alignment problem, a key challenge in understanding human mobility patterns. For instance, the problem can help answer the question: "Does a person who often visits a particular store on Fridays also visit another store on other weekdays?" To that end, we introduce a model called Hopper, which is designed to perform multi-hop inference to extract meaningful, hidden patterns from mobility data by leveraging the interconnections between locations and time periods. Hopper's effectiveness is demonstrated through its performance on two real-world datasets, which shows significant improvement over existing state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, Hopper is shown to be particularly effective in extracting rich information related to the motif (or pattern) being searched, which is a critical capability for any aligned alignment model to possess.

This theoretical report examines the production of charged leptons, along with $b$-quark pairs, within the context of the Standard Model. Cross-sections have been calculated for both experimental scenarios where the W boson is produced independently and when it is a part of a certain type of double gauge boson interaction. Calculations were made utilizing unitarity approximation for transverse momentum ranges of both W and lepton final states of up to 100 GeV. Research found that in experiments with 35 fb^-1 of data, a certain type of double gauge boson interaction can be detected at a 5 sigma confidence level, with mass measurements having an accuracy of 0.01 GeV. Additionally, we determined that unitarity approximation is effective for ranges of transverse momentum at least up to 60 GeV for W boson, 65 GeV for charged leptons, and 70 GeV for $b$-quark pairs.

This paper introduces a novel interaction method for controlling Telepresence robots using a wireless headset with a speech interface. A user study involved 10 participants instructing a Telepresence robot via voice commands through a wireless headset and assessing their Quality of Experience. Our interactive evaluation method yields a notable distinction and offers recommendations for improving Telepresence robot control by identifying the key factors that affect QoE. Notably, our research uncovered new QoE factors, such as the complexity of commands and spatial human awareness capabilities, which were demonstrated to have a significant impact on QoE levels. Moreover, our analysis highlights the main contributors to the variability in QoE reports.

This paper presents a basic overview of Bayesian hierarchical linear models, focusing on their application in social science data analysis. The presentation includes detailed explanations of model formulation, mathematical representation, computational modeling, and graphical analysis, aiming to provide a comprehensive understanding of this statistical methodology for readers with limited statistical background.

We introduce a numerical model of the Mafia game that operates under two distinct gameplay frameworks: one based on probability and the other on expectation. Although both models yield similar outcomes, they produce differing levels of covariance in the winners' probabilities, which varies inversely with the number of games played. Ultimately, we compare these frameworks' performance through simulated gaming tournaments.

This study explores the development of giant planets in a planet-forming disk that experiences an unusual phenomenon - the simultaneous growth of twin planets - an aspect often overlooked in traditional theories. We investigate the effects of gas accumulation in the early stages of a planetary system, and specifically how the simultaneous growth of massive twin planets affects the surrounding gas and material in the planet-forming disk. We analyze this through a range of theoretical simulations, considering the planetary masses and separations as variables. Our investigation into the planetary development reveals that in a planet-forming disk where the mass is evenly distributed, large gas-giant planets will develop simultaneously, but those in a disk where the mass is unevenly distributed will differ in size. We also found that in a planet-forming disk where the mass is concentrated at the center, one planet will dominate in size over its counterpart, but all massive gas-giant planets will form in a similar way, regardless of their separation. In a planet-forming disk where the mass is centered but with spiral arms, large gas-giant planets will develop simultaneously, but those in a disk where the mass is centered but with spiral arms will differ in size. We also found that in a planet-forming disk where the mass is centered but with spiral arms, large gas-giant planets will develop simultaneously, but those in a disk where the mass is centered but with spiral arms will differ in size.

The ability of electrons to move between different carbon nanotubes has been well documented, but the role of phonons in facilitating this movement remains unclear. In this study, we investigated how phonons contribute to electron transfer between carbon nanotubes through a combination of theoretical calculations and experimental measurements. By creating a film of carbon nanotubes with specific chiral indices and conducting photoemission spectroscopy, we identified electronic interactions between adjacent nanotubes.
